title: Combinatorial mosaics dissect the residue level basis of ACE2 binding divergence between SARS-CoV-2 and RaTG13
abstract: Abstract The spike proteins of SARS-CoV-2 and the closely related bat coronavirus RaTG13 differ in their binding affinity of human ACE2. This is due to differences in the receptor binding domain (RBD), the region primarily responsible for ACE2 binding, which are only 89% identical on the amino acid level, compared to 96% for the remainder of their genomes. Here, we constructed a combinatorial library of RBD mosaics containing combinations of 18 amino acid differences between SARS-CoV-2 and RaTG13 and measured human ACE2 binding using yeast surface display and fluorescence-activated cell sorting. The mosaics revealed a broad range of binding phenotypes. The effects on ACE2 binding were concentrated at eight positions, including all six variable positions that directly contact ACE2. Although the SARS-CoV-2 spike binds human ACE2 stronger than RaTG13 spike, the SARS-CoV-2 residues Q493 and Q498 each reduced ACE2 binding relative to RaTG13’s tyrosines. By measuring the effects of these residues across many combinations of other sequence differences, we identified sequence context dependence for residues 493 and 498, finding that the deleterious effects of Q493 and Q498 were attenuated by the SARS-CoV-2 residues at positions 483, 484, and 494. Together, these results provide a residue-level account of the sequence differences underlying the difference in ACE2 binding by SARS-CoV-2 and RaTG13 RBDs, including which differences have the largest effect and which depend on sequence context. This work demonstrates that mosaic libraries provide a robust approach for resolving the contributions of sequence differences across diverse backgrounds. Significance Statement Closely related proteins can differ greatly in function. Identifying which sequence differences underlie the difference in phenotype can be difficult. We built a large library of receptor binding domains that independently combined 18 differences between SARS-CoV-2 and the related bat coronavirus RaTG13 and measured their relative binding to human ACE2. Most of the difference in binding was concentrated to eight positions, and the effects of two of these positions, 493 and 498, changed depending on nearby amino acids. These results show that combinatorial mosaic libraries can resolve functional differences between homologous proteins at the residue level while also revealing context dependent effects.

title: The α-helix-facilitating amino acid sequence EAAAK dramatically increases the antiviral activity of SARS-CoV-2 fusion-inhibitory peptides via the endosome fusion pathway
abstract: ABSTRACT The SARS-CoV-2 fusion-inhibitory lipopeptide IPB29 features a unique design incorporating the α-helix-promoting EAAAK sequence as a rigid linker between the peptide backbone and the conjugated lipid, exhibiting greatly improved antiviral activity compared to lipopeptides with conventional flexible linkers. Here, we characterized its mechanism of action and uncovered several critical insights. First, IPB29 remained the most potent inhibitor of emerging Omicron subvariants compared to IPB24 and IPB28, which share the same peptide sequence but employ flexible polyethylene glycol or glycine-serine repeat linker. Notably, this enhanced potency was abolished in Vero E6 cells stably expressing TMPRSS2, where viral entry occurs via the plasma membrane fusion pathway. Visualization using FITC-labeled lipopeptides demonstrated that IPB29 binds to and enters target cells more efficiently. Subsequently, we generated two unconjugated template peptides, P43 (containing EAAAK) and P37 (lacking EAAAK). P43 exhibited superior inhibitory activity compared to P37 in Huh-7 and 293T/ACE2 cells, but not in Vero E6-TMPRSS2 cells. Both peptides showed comparable efficacy in blocking S protein-driven cell-cell fusion. Although P43 displayed enhanced α-helicity relative to P37, both peptides exhibited similar target-binding affinities. Instead, the cellular uptake of P43 was markedly more efficient, further supporting that the improved antiviral effect is attributable to the inhibition of the viral endosomal fusion pathway. Collectively, our studies provide molecular insights into the antiviral mechanism of IPB29 and propose the short EAAAK sequence as a generalizable strategy for enhancing the efficacy of peptide-based therapeutics. IMPORTANCE The development of effective therapeutics against SARS-CoV-2 remains an urgent priority. IPB29, a potent broad-spectrum lipopeptide fusion inhibitor currently in clinical trials, requires mechanistic elucidation. Here, we demonstrate that the C-terminal EAAAK motif in IPB29—originally designed as a rigid linker connecting the peptide backbone to the lipid moiety—is critical for its antiviral activity and functions via the endosomal fusion pathway. These findings reveal a generalizable strategy for optimizing antiviral drug design.

title: In silico and in vitro immunogenicity risk assessment of process- and product-related protein impurities reported in adenoviral-vectored COVID-19 vaccines.
abstract: Process-related protein impurities (PRPIs) such as host cell proteins (HCPs) in biologic products have been associated with unexpected immune responses, adverse events, and the discontinuation of clinical programs. While an HCP threshold of 100 ng/mg (PPM) is considered to be 'acceptable', that threshold may be too high if individual impurities have strong intrinsic immunogenicity or, in contrast, may be overly cautious if many of the HCP impurities have low immunogenicity. In silico methods for predicting the immunogenicity of PRI and HCP may help triage higher risk from lower risk entities. We explored this hypothesis by selecting candidate impurities from a published list of over 1,800 HEK-derived HCPs and adenoviral Product Related Impurities (PRIs) that were detected in high abundance in Chimp Adenovirus (AdV)-vectored COVID vaccine lots, for in silico and in vitro evaluation. The results of human donor peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC)-based assays were well aligned with in silico estimates. These orthogonal approaches, when combined, have the potential to identify process impurities that should be removed to remove prior to submission of a drug product for approval regulatory authorities. In addition, the in silico and in vitro approach described here provides a framework for improving the overall safety of biologic products.

title: Maternal Depression, Childhood Resting-State Brain Connectivity, and Adolescent Depression During the COVID-19 Outbreak.
abstract: Adolescents of mothers with a history of depression are at increased risk for developing depression themselves. These adolescents may have been especially vulnerable to depression under conditions of stress, such as the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. To understand the complex processes involved in the transmission of maternal depression risk to adolescent offspring in the context of stress, we examined potential mediating and moderating factors that link maternal depression history and offspring depressive symptoms, including resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) and mothers' depressive symptoms, in 85 adolescents during the pandemic. Adolescents' prepandemic rs-FC between the posterior and anterior cingulate cortices (PCC-ACC) moderated the association between maternal depression history and adolescents' symptoms during the pandemic, such that maternal depression history predicted adolescents' symptoms only in youths with heightened PCC-ACC rs-FC. Mothers' depressive symptoms during the pandemic mediated and moderated the link between maternal depression history and adolescents' symptoms. Mothers with a history of depression had greater depressive symptoms early during the pandemic, which were further associated with offspring depressive symptoms. Additionally, maternal depression history predicted depressive symptoms in adolescents whose mothers had lower depressive symptoms during the pandemic. Findings speak to the mediating and moderating processes in the transmission of maternal depression risk to adolescent offspring in the context of the pandemic.

title: Impact of Community Factors on Mental and Physical Health During Successive Waves of COVID-19 Pandemic in China.
abstract: This study examined how community factors impacted well-being during the COVID-19 pandemic in China. Data were collected at two time points: Time 1 (T1) in September 2021 (N = 992) when COVID-19 cases stabilized, and Time 2 (T2) in January 2023 (N = 497) during a sudden outbreak of new infected cases. At T1, perceived community safety and sense of community directly affected depression, anxiety, and physical health symptoms, with sense of community partially mediating these effects. At T2, community factors at T1 continued to impact depression, anxiety, and physical health symptoms. Sense of community at T1 partially mediated the link between community safety at T1 and mental health at T2. Higher income and older age were associated with a stronger sense of community, better perceived community safety, and improved health. Policymakers should consider the impact of community factors on well-being during health crises.

source_records.abstract: This study examined how community factors impacted well-being during the COVID-19 pandemic in China. Data were collected at two time points: Time 1 (T1) in September 2021 (N = 992) when COVID-19 cases stabilized, and Time 2 (T2) in January 2023 (N = 497) during a sudden outbreak of new infected cases. At T1, perceived community safety and sense of community directly affected depression, anxiety, and physical health symptoms, with sense of community partially mediating these effects. At T2, community factors at T1 continued to impact depression, anxiety, and physical health symptoms. Sense of community at T1 partially mediated the link between community safety at T1 and mental health at T2. Higher income and older age were associated with a stronger sense of community, better perceived community safety, and improved health. Policymakers should consider the impact of community factors on well-being during health crises.

title: Impact of COVID-19 Restrictions on Estimating Causal Effects: Fluoroquinolones and Tendon Rupture.
abstract: Purpose The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted healthcare services, potentially affecting causal effect estimation using real-world data. As a case study, we replicated a cohort study using Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum to evaluate whether pandemic-related disruptions influenced the measured association between fluoroquinolone use and tendon rupture. Methods We included adults initiating fluoroquinolones/cephalosporins during 1 January 2006-31 March 2023. Four analyses compared treatment effect estimates using different periods for exposure and outcome ascertainment: pre-pandemic only, pre-pandemic exposure with follow-up extending through the pandemic, all available data and post-pandemic only. We estimated hazard ratios (HRs) for tendon rupture using Cox regression. Results Among 891 968 fluoroquinolone users and 895 229 cephalosporin users, fluoroquinolone users had more comorbidities than cephalosporin users in the pre-pandemic period but fewer in the post-pandemic period. Pre-pandemic analysis showed an increased risk of tendon rupture associated with fluoroquinolones (Propensity score weighted [PSW]-HR: 1.94; 95% CI: 1.46-2.59), consistent with previous evidence. Estimates using all available data were similar for the overall study period (PSW-HR: 1.91; 95% CI: 1.46-2.51) and the pre-pandemic period (PSW-HR: 1.96; 95% CI: 1.47-2.61) but were less precise during/post-pandemic period (PSW-HR: 1.57; 95% CI: 0.72-3.41) with no evidence of a period-treatment interaction (PSW-HR: 0.80; 95% CI: 0.35-1.84). Post-pandemic analysis showed very few events among cephalosporin users but not fluoroquinolone users with a larger but imprecise estimate (PSW-HR: 3.32; 95% CI: 0.62-17.72). Conclusion In this case study, there was no clear evidence that pandemic-related healthcare disruptions materially altered causal estimates, albeit with limited power to detect differences between before and during/post-pandemic effects. Studies using real-world data across the pandemic should routinely examine temporal changes in baseline characteristics and outcome incidence.

title: "They could just come, they peep, then they get back": COVID-19 patients' experiences of care in isolation in Nairobi, Kenya
abstract: Isolation is a core measure of outbreak control, yet it reduces patients' contact with health workers and removes the support of family. During the COVID-19 pandemic, health workers became the main human contact for isolated patients while themselves contending with fear of infection and stigma. Little is known about how patients in sub-Saharan Africa experienced health workers' conduct under these conditions. This study explored how adults isolated with COVID-19 in Nairobi, Kenya, experienced interactions with health workers. I conducted a qualitative descriptive study using in-depth interviews with 15 adults who had recovered from COVID-19 after hospital isolation in Nairobi between 2020 and 2022. Participants were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling and interviewed in February and March 2023. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, and the resulting codes were mapped onto the Bohren et al. typology of mistreatment. Four themes were developed. First, some health workers offered attentive care, giving patients hope through encouragement and reassurance. Second, contact was brief and distant, a pattern that health workers themselves attributed to fear of infection. Third, care was organised around routine monitoring, so that deterioration and emotional distress often went unnoticed. Fourth, some patients encountered ridicule of their distress and perceived that patients were treated unequally. Most experiences corresponded to existing domains of the typology but distancing driven by fear of infection did not. Isolation increased patients' dependence on health workers at the same time as it created conditions that drew health workers away from them. Fear-driven distancing emerged as an additional domain of mistreatment in outbreak settings. Unaddressed, these patterns may compromise patient safety and weaken the trust on which outbreak responses depend. Preparedness plans should set minimum contact standards for isolated patients, include psychosocial assessment in routine monitoring and address health workers' fear of infection.

title: Inflammatory Biomarkers as Predictors of In-Hospital Mortality in Critically Ill COVID-19 Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Aim Inflammatory biomarkers have been proposed as prognostic indicators in COVID‐19; however, their prognostic associations within critically ill ICU‐admitted patients remain of interest. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of selected inflammatory biomarkers with in‐hospital mortality and their discriminatory performance among critically ill COVID‐19 patients. Methods In this retrospective cohort study, 244 adult patients with confirmed COVID‐19 pneumonia admitted to the ICU between August 2020 and June 2021 were analyzed. Disease severity was assessed using the ISARIC 4 C Mortality Score. Associations between inflammatory biomarkers and mortality were evaluated using univariable and multivariable logistic regression, and discriminatory performance was assessed using ROC curve analysis. Results The in‐hospital mortality rate was 90.6%. ESR and LDH levels were significantly higher in non‐survivors. In a biomarker‐restricted multivariable logistic regression model, ESR (OR 1.023 per 1 mm/h increase; 95% CI 1.004–1.042; p = 0.016) and LDH (OR 1.002 per 1 U/L increase; 95% CI 1.000–1.003; p = 0.009) remained significantly associated with in‐hospital mortality after mutual adjustment for the other prespecified inflammatory biomarkers. LDH demonstrated good discriminatory performance (AUC 0.725; 95% CI 0.645–0.805). ESR showed modest discriminatory performance (AUC 0.646; 95% CI 0.559–0.732). Conclusion ESR and LDH remained significantly associated with in‐hospital mortality after adjustment for the other prespecified inflammatory biomarkers. These findings suggest that ESR and LDH may provide adjunctive prognostic information in critically ill ICU patients; however, they should be interpreted in the context of the biomarker‐restricted model and the limited adjustment set. Confirmation in larger prospective studies incorporating established clinical prognostic factors is warranted.

title: Depression, anxiety, and stress at different time frames in relation to COVID-19 disease course: a Flemish observational study
abstract: Introduction Psychological distress can impact the course of viral infections such as COVID-19. This study aimed to examine how depression, anxiety, and stress, which occurred before and during COVID-19 infection, are associated with COVID-19 disease course (number of symptoms and duration of symptoms) in Flemish outpatients. Methods In early 2022, a two-wave web-based survey was administered to 3,025 adults who had a positive COVID-19 PCR test. Psychological distress was assessed using the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21) and COVID-19 disease course with a set of self-constructed items. Generalized linear models were used to evaluate the associations. Several control variables were included in the analysis, such as vaccination status, comorbidities, and previous SARS-CoV-2 infection. Results Across all time frames, psychological distress showed consistent, statistically significant associations with both aspects of the COVID-19 disease course (with the exception of psychopharmaceutical use 3 years before COVID-19 infection and duration of symptoms), albeit with small to moderate effect sizes typical of psychological research. Across all time frames, anxiety during infection showed the largest point estimates with number of symptoms (IRR: 1.20, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.23) and duration of symptoms (OR: 1.79, 95% CI 1.55 to 2.07). However, there was no statistical evidence that these associations differed in magnitude from other types of distress. When focusing on psychological distress before COVID-19 infection, anxiety short-term before infection had the largest point estimate for number of symptoms (IRR: 1.13, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.16) and duration of symptoms (OR: 1.40, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.61), although we did not find evidence of differences in effects across types of distress. Conclusion All measures of psychological distress were significantly associated with worse COVID-19 outcomes, except for the association between psychopharmaceutical use 3 years before COVID-19 infection and duration of symptoms. The magnitude of effects showed a consistent trend whereby anxiety short-term before and during COVID-19 infection showing the strongest associations, though not significantly different. This observational survey study has a few notable limitations associated with measurement and casual inferences, including those related to recall bias and self-report of both independent and outcome variables. Further research is needed to clarify these associations in a causal and mechanistic framework.

title: Immune analysis of long covid to inform rational choices in diagnostic testing and therapeutics – Working out the Immunology of Long COvid (WILCO) - COV-LT2-0027
abstract: Plain English Summary The WILCO cohort ('Working out the Immunology of Long Covid'), both adult and paediatric, is novel in terms of being a large, UK cohort of individuals who were largely non-hospitalised during their acute infections and have here been followed longitudinally and in detail, at the level of symptom profile and immunological parameters. Data from this cohort establish a number of key points. This is a large cohort, many of whom have been persistently unwell with multi-system, multi-organ disease for 3-4 years. Longitudinal analysis shows that most symptoms show little improvement across an interval of more than a year. WILCO participants are indicative of Long Covid (LC) trends nationally and globally insofar as many have lost jobs or changed to part-time work as a consequence of their disability. We were able to identify a number of immune correlates of LC, likely contributing to immunopathogenesis: altered immunoglobulin isotype profiles, altered T cell immunity to spike, altered patterns of autoimmunity and altered B cell plasmablast and natural killer cell subsets. Our findings aid in defining the mechanisms underpinning Long Covid, offer potential directions for therapeutic trials and also for diagnostic tests. Executive Summary Background: During the past 4-years, much has been learnt around the world about Long Covid – the chronic, post-viral sequelae persisting more than 12 weeks and, generally, some years, after COVID-19. It is estimated that there are some 400-million sufferers globally and by Office for National Statistics (ONS) Data, 2-million in the UK. These individuals are unable to regain their baseline health, often suffering disability that makes it impossible to return fully to their former employment. This large, new disease burden has profound implications for the workforce, the NHS, and for healthcare planning and provision. This proposal made the point that this is hypothesised to be an immune/inflammatory-mediated disease process, and that we need immune analysis in order to understand the basis of the condition, design diagnostic tests, and build an understanding of the likely approaches for therapeutic drug trials. The work has gone well. The cohort was termed ‘WILCO’ for ‘Working Out the Immunology of Long Covid’ and we were able to recruit nearly 1000 individuals into the cohort. This is a novel and informative Long Covid study cohort since it comprises people with well-characterised Long Covid symptoms, in many cases affected now for 3-4 years, and with their condition deriving from infections across each of the COVID-19 variant waves: ancestral Wuhan Hu-1 (the 2020-wave), Alpha, Delta, and Omicron. Because the analysis is longitudinal, we have been able to understand the persistence of symptoms, their long-term effects and immune correlates. We have also been able to relate symptoms and immune parameters in the adult cohort to our parallel, paediatric Long Covid cohort. Study aims and methods: Our goal was to work towards development of clear, diagnostic tests through high-granularity immunological analysis for biomarker discovery. Analysis would use peripheral blood samples, the study groups comprising: i) Healthy controls, ii) Individuals who had confirmed COVID-19 with rapid recovery and iii) Individuals who meet the criteria for Long Covid - greater than 12 weeks from the start of acute COVID-19 infection without recovery back to baseline health. iv) We would relate findings in this adult, largely non-hospitalised cohort to an additional cohort - a paediatric cohort recruited through referral to the Paediatric Long Covid clinical service at KCL and the Evelina Hospital. The specific questions to be addressed in the lab using cohort blood samples were as follows: • Analysis of white blood cell immune subsets using an approach termed multi-parameter flow cytometry. That is, measuring the specific profile of lymphocyte subsets contributing to immunity using fluorescently labelled antibodies. We would thus compare immune subsets in people with Long Covid relative to people who made a full recovery from acute infection to investigate perturbations in immune subsets. • In related lab analyses, we would make RNA from blood to analyse the differential programmes driving immune subsets in Long Covid and fully recovered controls • We would correlate disease symptoms with specific patterns of antibody and/or T cell autoimmunity, addressing the hypothesis that the origins of Long Covid may be partly through the ability of the virus to drive an autoimmune condition whereby the immune system erroneously attacks cells in the body. Results and key findings: Since the start of the award we have achieved each of our milestones. A cohort of nearly 1000 was consented and recruited at Imperial College London, detailed symptom and clinical history questionnaires were completed at two longitudinal timepoints, analysed and clustered by machine learning, participants gave blood samples which were used in detailed immunological investigations as described above, and these immune parameters have illuminated understanding of the processes underlying Long Covid, offering potential tests and clues to therapeutic approaches. The initial deliverable was to establish the infrastructure to recruit, build and characterise a UK-based, largely non-hospitalised, Long Covid research cohort and recovered controls, representative of the experience of the majority of Long Covid sufferers. Participants were recruited in response to adverts posted through community newsletters, social media, Long Covid support networks, general and Long Covid clinics. All participants completed a detailed, questionnaire-based symptom history using a validated, published, protocol. In most cases this was done at 2 timepoints separated by 12-18 months. This follow-up comprised a second, expanded questionnaire and additional blood sample collection, enabling longitudinal analysis of immune responses and the progression or resolution of symptoms over time. Some participants were thus investigated at 3-4 years from the initial infection, making this a novel, longitudinal cohort of what has sometimes been referred to as ‘Long-Long Covid.’ At the follow-up 2nd visit, 90% of LC participants who had experienced persistent, Long Covid symptoms at visit 1, continued to suffer from these symptoms, with only 9% reporting symptom resolution. As understanding of the scale of the LC problem grew, it became apparent, for example through Office for National Statistics (ONS) data and through engagement with the PPI group and with the Long Covid Support charity, that affected individuals may often face problems with employment and housing as a consequence of their condition. Additional questions were introduced into the Visit 2 questionnaire for the WILCO cohort to investigate this. In this cohort 69% of participants reported a change in work status, with 88% of these attributing the change to medical reasons. In contrast, only 22% of participants in the Full Recovery (FR) group reported a change in work status, with just 5% of those changes due to medical reasons. Before the pandemic, the primary work status in both the LC and FR groups had been ‘full-time’, with 67% of LC participants and 61% of FR participants working full-time. Part-time employment was less common, reported by 21% in the LC group and 20% in the FR group. We are finishing off our analysis of the paediatric Long Covid cohort to see whether mechanisms are similar in children. In summary, this proposal has delivered on its goals. We are now looking to apply our findings in the context of therapeutic drug trials that may address the problem of a persistent reservoir of uncleared virus driving this disease.

source_records.abstract: Plain English Summary The WILCO cohort ('Working out the Immunology of Long Covid'), both adult and paediatric, is novel in terms of being a large, UK cohort of individuals who were largely non-hospitalised during their acute infections and have here been followed longitudinally and in detail, at the level of symptom profile and immunological parameters. Data from this cohort establish a number of key points. This is a large cohort, many of whom have been persistently unwell with multi-system, multi-organ disease for 3-4 years. Longitudinal analysis shows that most symptoms show little improvement across an interval of more than a year. WILCO participants are indicative of Long Covid (LC) trends nationally and globally insofar as many have lost jobs or changed to part-time work as a consequence of their disability. We were able to identify a number of immune correlates of LC, likely contributing to immunopathogenesis: altered immunoglobulin isotype profiles, altered T cell immunity to spike, altered patterns of autoimmunity and altered B cell plasmablast and natural killer cell subsets. Our findings aid in defining the mechanisms underpinning Long Covid, offer potential directions for therapeutic trials and also for diagnostic tests. Executive Summary Background: During the past 4-years, much has been learnt around the world about Long Covid – the chronic, post-viral sequelae persisting more than 12 weeks and, generally, some years, after COVID-19. It is estimated that there are some 400-million sufferers globally and by Office for National Statistics (ONS) Data, 2-million in the UK. These individuals are unable to regain their baseline health, often suffering disability that makes it impossible to return fully to their former employment. This large, new disease burden has profound implications for the workforce, the NHS, and for healthcare planning and provision. This proposal made the point that this is hypothesised to be an immune/inflammatory-mediated disease process, and that we need immune analysis in order to understand the basis of the condition, design diagnostic tests, and build an understanding of the likely approaches for therapeutic drug trials. The work has gone well. The cohort was termed ‘WILCO’ for ‘Working Out the Immunology of Long Covid’ and we were able to recruit nearly 1000 individuals into the cohort. This is a novel and informative Long Covid study cohort since it comprises people with well-characterised Long Covid symptoms, in many cases affected now for 3-4 years, and with their condition deriving from infections across each of the COVID-19 variant waves: ancestral Wuhan Hu-1 (the 2020-wave), Alpha, Delta, and Omicron. title: Clinical characteristics and efficacy of vaccination on severity in hospitalized patients with COVID-19 during different pandemic periods
abstract: To characterize clinical severity of COVID-19 in hospitalized patients during pandemic periods and to assess the effect of vaccination on disease course. Materials and methods. Single-centre retrospective cohort study of 11,203 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 in 2020– 2023 (112,455 bed-days). Clinical severity was graded on a four-level respiratory failure scale: «none»; «oxygen mask/cannula»; «noninvasive ventilation» (NIV); «invasive mechanical ventilation» (IMV). Bayesian hierarchical ordinal regression was fitted with covariates: age, Elixhauser comorbidity index, vaccination, previous-day respiratory failure, pandemic day and disease days. Statistical analysis was performed with programming languages R 4.6.0 and Stan 2.38.0. The 28-day cumulative risk of respiratory failure was up to 50 % in the first wave, up to 80 % in the period of Alpha variant predominance, > 90 % (unvaccinated) and ≤ 65 % (vaccinated) in the period of Delta variant predominance, and ≤ 25 % in the Omicron. During predominance of Delta variant, the probability of NIV/IMV reached 25–30 % in older unvaccinated patients with comorbidities compared to ≤ 4.5 % in vaccinated ones; during predominance of Omicron variants it was < 1 %, though up to 20 % still required oxygen. After standardization, vaccination was associated with a lower cumulative risk from September 2021 to March 2022, peaking in December 2021: -24.3 % (95 % CI (-17,6; -30,6)). Respiratory failure severity varied by pandemic period, and vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 had a protective effect in hospitalized patients.

title: The detection paradox: How COVID-19 surveillance patterns shifted from lower-income to more affluent neighborhoods in Miami-Dade County.
abstract: Passive disease surveillance systems may systematically undercount burden in low-resource minority neighborhoods, yet fine-scale evidence of this phenomenon remains limited. We examined spatiotemporal patterns of reported COVID-19 cases across Miami-Dade County's diverse neighborhoods and investigated which socioeconomic and demographic characteristics predicted areas of elevated and suppressed case rates. In an ecological, cross-sectional analysis of 491,769 geocoded cases across 1,831 census block groups from March 2020 to May 2021, we applied negative binomial regression with spatial eigenvector filtering and Getis-Ord Gi* hot spot analysis across five pandemic periods aligned with major policy shifts. The analysis revealed a detection paradox. Early hot spots concentrated in lower-income census block groups (median household income: $52,022-$55,676), but by September 2020, hot spots had shifted to more affluent areas (median: $77,069). Historically Black neighborhoods along the I-95 corridor emerged as persistent cold spots despite multiple structural risk factors: lower incomes, reduced insurance coverage, and limited healthcare access. From Period 3 onward, predominantly Black census block groups showed significantly lower reported rates (incidence rate ratio [IRR]: 0.991-0.995, p < 0.001). Household overcrowding was tested but retained in no final model. These paradoxical patterns suggest that as testing expanded, surveillance increasingly tracked healthcare utilization rather than transmission. What appeared as neighborhood "protection" likely reflected barriers to testing access shaped by transportation constraints, work schedule inflexibility, and historical relationships with medical institutions. Census block group analysis revealed these dynamics obscured at broader geographic scales. The findings challenge the assumption that reported case rates approximate true disease burden and have direct implications for emergency response planning: surveillance systems require complementary detection streams, risk-adjusted monitoring for underdetection, and targeted outreach where poverty and limited access to testing are concentrated but reported rates are low.

title: EFFICACY OF IVERMECTIN IN COVID-19: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF RANDOMISED CONTROLLED TRIALS
abstract: Ivermectin, an antiparasitic with a long safety record, was proposed early in the COVID-19 pandemic as a repurposed antiviral after it inhibited SARS-CoV-2 replication in cell culture. This review, which reports no new data, examines the published randomised controlled trials of ivermectin in COVID-19 together with the pharmacology, meta-analyses and safety literature. Small early trials gave mixed and sometimes favourable signals, whereas larger, better-designed placebo-controlled trials in outpatients found no clinically meaningful benefit on recovery, hospitalisation or death. Favourable pooled estimates depended heavily on low-quality or later discredited studies. Concentrations needed for antiviral effect are hard to reach at approved doses. Ivermectin cannot be recommended for COVID-19 outside trials.

title: A Severe COVID-19-associated hNTPDase2 Variant is Enzymatically Inactive
abstract: Abstract Nucleoside triphosphate diphosphohydrolases (NTPDases) regulate extracellular nucleotide levels and thereby modulate nucleotide signalling. Increased extracellular ATP levels and altered nucleotide signalling have been reported in patients with moderate to severe COVID-19. A specific variant in the gene encoding human NTPDase2 (hNTPDase2), classified in ClinVar as likely pathogenic, has been reported in patients with severe COVID-19. Sequence analysis of this variant revealed a single G nucleotide deletion at position 1170 of the coding sequence, resulting in a frameshift and a premature stop codon. The predicted protein is truncated from 495 to 408 amino acids and lacks ACR5, the C-terminal transmembrane domain, and a few other functionally important residues. We generated the corresponding variant, referred to as hN2COV, by site-directed mutagenesis and expressed it in CHO-S cells. Expression of the FLAG-tagged hN2COV was confirmed by western blotting. Whereas the reference hNTPDase2 efficiently hydrolyzed ATP and UTP, no detectable activity was observed for hN2COV with ATP, ADP, UTP, or UDP. These findings identify hN2COV as a loss-of-function variant and suggest that loss of NTPDase2 activity may contribute to altered extracellular nucleotide signalling in individuals carrying this variant.

title: Blood biomarkers of long COVID: A cross-sectional evaluation of key cytokines and the coordination of inflammation.
abstract: Introduction Long COVID is a complex pathophysiological condition linked to a heterogenous symptom profile. Dysregulation of 1) immunological and inflammatory responses, 2) endothelial/vascular function, and 3) metabolic and clotting processes have been identified; however, there remains a lack of clinically validated diagnostic biomarkers. The study aim was to investigate dysregulation of cytokines, chemokines and growth factors in confirmed Long COVID cases grouped by disease severity. Methods One-hundred-and-twenty-seven participants provided venous blood samples for cytokine profiling utilising Luminex assays. Participants were grouped into those with no knowledge of SARS-CoV-2 infection (n = 21), acute infection within 3-months (n = 22), spontaneous resolvers (>3-months, n = 21) and those with confirmed Long COVID (n = 63). Long COVID severity was grouped according to the post-COVID-19 functional status (PCFS) and defined as those with negligible (4A; n = 9), mild (4B; n = 20), moderate (4C; n = 24), and severe limitations (4D; n = 10). Cytokines were assessed for normality using Shapiro-Wilk tests and differences measured between groups using Kruskal-Wallis tests. Pairwise correlation and principal component analysis were performed. Results Interleukin-12 (p40/p70) was 22% greater in the Long COVID group (Median [IQR]: 58 [49] pg/mL, p = 0.046) and 30% greater in the acutely infected group (64 [36] pg/mL; p = 0.039) against non-infected controls (45 [25] pg/mL). Following PCFS classification, fibroblast growth factor-basic was 25% lower in Long COVID 4B versus spontaneous resolvers (24 [7] vs. 32 [24] pg/mL; p = 0.025). Pairwise correlation differences demonstrated that three Long COVID subgroups had strong, positive associations between cytokines when compared to non-infected controls; however, PCA was unable to determine any coordinated cytokine variation that was group specific. Discussion and conclusions Elevated interleukin-12 (p40/p70) and reduced basic fibroblast growth factor suggest persistent immune activation and possible subgroup-specific Long COVID; however, these findings were marginally significant and exploratory. A coordinated but partial immunological/inflammatory profile may exist in some of those with Long COVID, suggesting a rationale for subgrouping upon a biological, rather than self-report basis but larger longitudinal studies are required to confirm this hypothesis.

title: Does COVID-19 Vaccination Protect Against Post-COVID Cardiovascular Conditions?
abstract: Cardiovascular diseases, such as acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, and arrhythmias, have been associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection, representing an important cause of long-term morbidity and mortality. In addition to preventing primary infection, COVID-19 vaccination has emerged as a protective factor against post-COVID cardiovascular outcomes. This study aims to analyse the evidence supporting a causal relationship between COVID-19 vaccination and the prevention of post-COVID cardiovascular conditions, based on classical and contemporary epidemiological criteria, including the Bradford Hill criteria (BHC) and the sufficient component cause (SCC) model. A qualitative synthesis of the evidence was performed according to the nine BHC and the SCC model. Scientific evidence indicates that COVID-19 vaccination meets four of the nine BHC as a protective factor against post-COVID cardiovascular conditions, namely strength of association, consistency, temporality, and biological gradient. Three criteria, biological plausibility, coherence, and analogy, were partially met. Specificity and experimental evidence were not supported by the available literature. The SCC model highlights the fundamental role of vaccination as a preventive causal component. It also contributes to two criteria, strength of association and temporality, while emphasising the limitation of specificity in causal inference. COVID-19 vaccination has proven effective beyond the acute phase of the disease, with protection extending to a reduced risk of post-COVID cardiovascular conditions. Comprehensive immunisation strategies and reinfection prevention are essential to mitigate the burden of post-COVID conditions. Additional studies are needed to explore the underlying biological mechanisms, interactions, and the role of COVID-19 vaccination in preventing post-COVID complications.

title: Live-cell, single-molecule imaging resolves the dual nature of mRNA silencing by SARS-CoV-2 Nsp1
abstract: SARS-CoV-2 nonstructural protein 1 (Nsp1) is a conserved viral factor that potently silences host transcripts by binding ribosomes. Yet how it acts at the level of individual mRNAs remains unclear, with competing models arguing that Nsp1 blocks translation initiation, stalls ribosome elongation, cleaves mRNA, or does all three. Here, we use Nascent Chain Tracking to quantify in living cells how Nsp1 reshapes mRNA abundance and translation dynamics with single-molecule resolution. Using reporter transcripts that vary in UTR architecture, initiation mode, and open reading frame length, we find that Nsp1 mainly silences our reporter transcripts by reducing their numbers rather than inhibiting initiation. Two routes to Nsp1-mediated mRNA loss are identified, both requiring cap-dependent initiation: an early route acting during or shortly after initiation and a later route associated with downstream translation that depends in part on ZNF598. Together, these two mechanisms make Nsp1 an efficient and robust suppressor of host gene expression. We further find that reporters containing the SARS-CoV-2 UTRs remain susceptible to Nsp1-mediated mRNA loss, but the 5' and 3' UTRs cooperate to increase translation output. Neither viral UTR alone increased translation beyond the host reporter, whereas combining both UTRs substantially enhanced translation in the absence of Nsp1. Together, our results reveal that Nsp1 uses dual, cap-dependent routes to promote mRNA loss across the translation cycle, while the SARS-CoV-2 UTRs provide a cooperative translational advantage rather than robust protection from Nsp1.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Complications of Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) in Adult Patients With COVID-19 in Central and Eastern Europe: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a rescue therapy for severe COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). International datasets do not consistently report Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) separately. We aimed to assess mortality, clinical characteristics, and complications of ECMO-treated COVID-19 patients across the CEE region. MATERIAL AND METHODS We conducted a systematic review with single-arm meta-analyses of observational studies. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from January 2020 to August 2025 for studies reporting ECMO outcomes in adult (≥18 years) COVID-19 patients from CEE countries, with at least 10 ECMO-treated patients. Conference abstracts and overlapping cohorts were excluded. The study protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251077593). RESULTS Twelve studies included 802 patients from 6 countries. Pooled in-hospital mortality was 65% (95% CI 0.57-0.72; I2=70.6%; 10 studies; n=691), and ICU mortality was 61% (95% CI 0.47-0.74; I2=85.8%; 7 studies, n=526). Country-level in-hospital mortality estimates were 54% for the Czech Republic and 76% for Poland but were descriptive because of the small number of studies and wide CIs. Mean pre-ECMO mechanical ventilation duration was 4.8 days (95% CI 3.7-5.8; I2=4.4%), ECMO duration was 17.8 days (95% CI 12.8-22.9; I2=79.8%), and ICU length of stay was 23.6 days (95% CI 7.5-39.7; I2=92.6%). Serious bleeding occurred in 40% (95% CI 22-61%; I2=85.7%). Certainty was very low for all pooled outcomes. CONCLUSIONS These CEE-specific estimates provide regional benchmarks, but substantial heterogeneity and very low certainty limit international comparisons and country-level interpretation. Standardized regional registries, prospective multicenter data, harmonized complication reporting, and long-term outcome assessment are needed.

title: A 78-Year-Old Man With a Previously Stable Atherosclerotic Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Presenting With Impending Rupture Following COVID-19.
abstract: BACKGROUND Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) rupture is a life-threatening condition. Although elective repair is generally guided by aneurysm size, impending rupture can occur when rapid aneurysmal expansion or periaortic inflammatory changes develop before overt hemodynamic deterioration. This report describes the case of a 78-year-old man with a previously stable 43-mm atherosclerotic AAA who presented with impending rupture after coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). CASE REPORT A 78-year-old Japanese man with a known AAA under imaging surveillance developed fever and was diagnosed with COVID-19 by nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction testing. Seven days later, he was admitted for recurrent fever, cough, poor appetite, and elevated inflammatory markers. His medical history included hypertension, heavy smoking, advanced chronic kidney disease, and diffuse atherosclerotic disease. The aneurysm had shown minimal growth over 2 years, with a stable maximum short-axis diameter of approximately 43 mm on serial computed tomography. After admission, C-reactive protein levels initially decreased but rose again on hospital day 11, accompanied by new-onset mild low back pain and no marked blood pressure elevation or hemodynamic instability. Repeat non-contrast abdominal computed tomography performed 18 days after COVID-19 diagnosis demonstrated rapid AAA expansion from 43 mm to 51 mm within 2 months, with periaortic fat stranding, consistent with impending rupture. Urgent endovascular aneurysm repair was performed before hemodynamic deterioration. The postoperative course was stable, and the patient was discharged without ischemic or procedural complications. CONCLUSIONS This case shows that a previously stable AAA can abruptly destabilize after recent COVID-19. Repeat imaging should be considered when inflammatory markers rise or new symptoms occur, even when symptoms are mild.

title: Post-hospitalisation COVID-19 study: a national consortium to understand and improve long-term health outcomes (PHOSP-COVID) - COV0319
abstract: Plain English Summary The severity of illness following infection with COVID-19 has decreased because of public health policies, vaccination and acute anti-viral and anti-inflammatory therapies. However, in the wake of the pandemic post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 known as ‘long COVID’ has emerged. Long COVID is a chronic illness in people that continue to experience ongoing symptoms and disability. Background: In the wake of the pandemic post-acute sequelae of COVID-19, known as long COVID, have emerged. Long COVID is a chronic illness in people experiencing ongoing symptoms and disability beyond four weeks after infection (NICE 2020). PHOSP-COVID ( PHOSP.org ) is a UK consortium established in the summer 2020 comprising of leading multi-disciplinary researchers and clinicians, with patient, public and voluntary sector involvement (PPI), working together to understand and improve long-term health outcomes for adults who were discharged from hospital following COVID-19. We recruited adults discharged from hospital after COVID-19 between Feb 2020–March 2021 to three tiers of research: ‘Tier 1 which utilised use of routine health data, questionnaires, and a saliva sample for genetic testing; ‘Tier 2’ involving early (5 month) and later 12 month visits which included deep phenotyping with patient reported outcomes measures (PROMS) capturing physical symptoms, mental health, health related quality of life, and measures of cognitive impairment, device-measured 24h physical activity profiling, muscle strength, exercise capacity, frailty and organ impairment including clinical blood tests and lung function tests. A bioresource was collected sampling blood, urine, sputum and oral wash. For ‘Tier 3’ people from Tier 1 or Tier 2 were recalled for additional visits or procedures for example for more detailed immune tests and multi-organ magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). All participants were asked to consent to further follow-up for 25 years via linkage to their electronic healthcare records and to be re-contacted for further research. Cohort data are held in a Trusted Research Environment (TRE) and samples stored in a central biobank. Data and samples can be accessed upon request and subject to approvals from https://www.phosp.org/data-sample-request/ . These can be found on the website - https://www.phosp.org/publications - and include publications in Lancet and Lancet family of journals, Nature family of journals, Science Immunology, AJRCCM, Thorax, European Respiratory Journal. The early key findings were that at 5 months after hospital discharge from COVID-19, only about 30% of people self-reported that they had fully recovered. The proportion was similar after 1 year with only marginal improvement from 5 months to 1 year. Participants were less likely to have recovered if female, aged 35- 65 years old, body mass index >30, or they had multiple long-term conditions prior to COVID-19 or required mechanical ventilation whilst hospitalised. We found that the treatments given for the acute infection such as corticosteroids did not affect the likelihood of recovery consistent with the 6-month follow-up of the REMAP-CAP study. Through unsupervised cluster analysis, we identified the severity of physical and mental health largely grouped together whereas ‘brain-fog’ can occur on its own. Those with the most severe health impairments had evidence of persistent inflammation reflected by an elevated c-reactive protein. Multi-organ, multi-modality MRI revealed changes in the brain, lungs and kidneys but no significant increase in cardiac or liver abnormalities compared to controls. Normal electrocardiogram reliably excluded cardiac MRI abnormalities. People with a higher burden of multi-organ injury were more likely to report poor physical and mental recovery. With specific co-morbid conditions people with diabetes, cardiovascular disease or cardiovascular risk factors or pre-existing airway diseases had worse symptoms and physical outcomes up to 12 months after hospital discharge with COVID-19. In the lungs, the prevalence of interstitial lung abnormalities on thoracic computed tomography was estimated at 8.5%, which was associated with biomarkers of epithelial injury. We have found increased auto-antibodies and immunosenescence in people with long COVID compared to controls. Despite the predominately working-age population of the study, exercise capacity was reduced with increased frailty indices. Sleep pattern data derived from accelerometry showed decreased activity, increased sleep duration, but reduced quality with sleep regularity associated with breathlessness compared with non-COVID hospitalised patients. We identified two distinct biomarker profiles of inflammation and coagulation (fibrinogen, D dimer and CRP), which predict cognitive outcomes 6 and 12 months after COVID-19. Findings were replicated in a large-scale electronic health records dataset. This provides insights into the heterogeneous biology of post-COVID cognitive deficits. However, we did not find evidence to support ongoing neuropsychiatric symptoms are due to neural injury. Critically, psychiatric and cognitive symptoms appear to increase over the first 2-3 years post-hospitalisation due to both worsening of symptoms already present at 6 months and emergence of new symptoms. Early identification and interventions to promote cognitive recovery or to prevent cognitive decline are therefore needed to limit the functional and economic impacts of COVID-19. We are actively pursuing diagnostic and prognostic biomarker discovery. Our findings from sampling at the ~ 5-month point suggest that specific inflammatory pathways related to tissue damage identified in blood using O-link proteomics are implicated in subtypes of long COVID. These findings are being extended in further samples obtained at 1 year and with other platforms and other sample types. We have contributed to international efforts on long COVID genetics. We discovered an association of [the transcription factor] FOXP4 with long COVID, independent of its previously identified association with severe COVID-19. The signal was replicated in 9,500 long COVID cases and 798,835 population controls. Given the transcription factor FOXP4's role in lung physiology and pathology, our findings highlight the importance of lung function in the pathophysiology of long COVID. We have identified genetic evidence implicating shared pathogenetic pathways in thromboembolism and long COVID. However, in PHOSP-COVID chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension was an uncommon complication. PHOSP-COVID has undertaken 2 proof-of-concept randomised controlled trials: one completed for rehabilitation and another ongoing for anti-IL6 therapy for those people with evidence of ongoing systemic inflammation. Exercise-based rehabilitation improved short term exercise capacity in post-COVID syndrome following an acute hospitalisation and showed potential for beneficial immunomodulatory effects. Five-year follow-up is underway. Our analysis supports the need for proactive, stratified, comprehensive follow-up, particularly assessment and rehabilitation for adults after hospitalisation with COVID-19, showing these services are clinically and cost-effective. Key findings, including headline messages relevant to policy makers: Long COVID is common post-hospitalisation for acute COVID (this has been shown to be also the case in those that were not hospitalised in other studies). Effects are persistent and include multiple physical and mental health symptoms. Risk factors include female sex, multi-morbidity, middle-aged, increased body mass index and indices of deprivation. There is evidence of multi-organ damage, persistent inflammation, activated autoimmunity and immune aging. There are potential biomarkers in development that will support diagnosis and future precision medicine. Rehabilitation in appropriate groups of patients is beneficial. Therapeutic targets have been identified with some trials ongoing and others required. Conclusions and recommendations for further research: Future long COVID research needs to focus on fundamental understanding of underlying mechanisms, validated biomarkers with clinical utility, new therapies and care pathways to manage those with ongoing or emerging disease. The need for future pandemic preparedness and need for further research in long COVID and other post-infectious sequelae has been described in detail in the Covid Inquiry report and from our expert statements (Covid Inquiry 2025). Dissemination plans: A major strength of PHOSP-COVID is that patients, clinicians, and scientists worked together in 2020 to agree the priority research questions and throughout the study, there has been close engagement between the consortium, patients involved in the study and the wider public with a regular public newsletters, online seminars and lectures. During the first 2 years of the consortium, we held teaching sessions with professionals supported by the British thoracic Society. We work closely with the other national long COVID consortia and internationally with professional societies such as the European Respiratory Society. Our findings have been extensively published in the scientific literature with several papers to be published in the forthcoming years. Our work has been widely covered in national and international television, print media and online. Professor Brightling and Professor Evans presented at the UK Covid-19 Inquiry as expert witnesses on long COVID. PHOSP-COVID was a finalist for the MRC Impact Prize for Outstanding Team Impact award. Expected influence/impact: We have participated in meetings chaired by the DHSC secretary of state ahead of the formation of the SoS/ministerial-led long COVID Roundtable meetings in 2020-21. We co-authored the AMS report published in July 2020 and gave evidence to the House of Lords Science and technology committee on the Science of COVID-19 2020. We co-authored a report to SAGE and participated in SAGE. We are members of the National Long Covid Research Group. We have evaluated clinical and cost effectiveness of clinical care pathways, and contributed to NICE and NHS-England long COVID guidance for clinical care and rehabilitation. With patient groups we have presented to the all-parliamentary group for long COVID. source_records.title: Post-hospitalisation COVID-19 study: a national consortium to understand and improve long-term health outcomes (PHOSP-COVID) - COV0319
source_records.abstract: Plain English Summary The severity of illness following infection with COVID-19 has decreased because of public health policies, vaccination and acute anti-viral and anti-inflammatory therapies. However, in the wake of the pandemic post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 known as ‘long COVID’ has emerged. Long COVID is a chronic illness in people that continue to experience ongoing symptoms and disability. The PHOSP-COVID consortium was established in August 2020 and its aims are: i) to describe the impact of long COVID on people that were hospitalised with COVID-19 infection, ii) what features are associated either with good or poor recovery, iii) what is the underlying cause of long COVID, iv) is long COVID altered by treatments given for the acute infection and v) can we develop treatments for people with long COVID to improve recovery. The PHOSP-COVID consortium includes 83 hospitals, over 25 universities, 10+ patient groups and charities and 500+ researchers. We recruited people to three tiers of research: tier 1: questionnaires, use of routine data and a saliva sample for genetic testing, tier 2: an early (5 month) and later 12 month visit that included detailed questionnaires, exercise tests, sampling such as blood tests and tier 3 whereby people had additional visits for more detailed immune tests and magnetic resonance imaging. Recruitment has been completed across the 4 nations. 7935 participants were recruited to the study (Tier 1: 5231, Tier 2: 2704 with Tier 3 participants included in Tier 2). Patients, clinicians and scientists worked together on developing priority research questions and throughout the study, there has been close engagement between the consortium, patients involved in the study and the wider public. We found that at 5 months only about 30% of people that were hospitalised due to COVID-19 infection had fully recovered. This proportion was similar after 1 year with only marginal improvement from 5 months to 1 year. You were more likely not to have recovered if you were a woman, were between the ages of 35-65 years old, were obese, had multiple long-term conditions prior to COVID-19 infection or required mechanical ventilation whilst hospitalised. We found that the treatments given for the acute infection such as corticosteroids did not affect the likelihood of recovery. We found that the severity of symptoms largely grouped together except for ‘brain-fog’, which could occur on its own. Those with the most severe symptoms had evidence of persistent inflammation measured with a simple blood test called CRP. This measure is associated with a specific inflammatory pathway and with industry colleagues; we will be testing whether treatments targeting this pathway improve recovery. Magnetic resonance imaging in our participants showed changes in the brain, heart, lungs and liver. In the lungs, about 5% have evidence of early lung scarring on CT scans. We are looking at how these changes link to severity of disease and impairments in the immune response. We have found several important features in the immune response. In older people with long COVID the immune response is decreased, there is increased auto-immunity with activation of specific types of immune cells. We have found that exercise capacity is reduced and are testing whether in some people tailored exercise programmes might be helpful. We have also found that sleep disturbance after COVID-19 hospitalisation is associated with breathlessness, reduced lung function, anxiety and muscle weakness and this is likely to be a specific effect of COVID-19. Furthermore, we have found that two proteins, fibrinogen and D-Dimer were raised at the time of Covid-19 suggesting that blood clots during COVID-19 may be a cause of ongoing cognitive problems in patients hospitalized with COVID-19. More detailed work is ongoing looking into effects on all the organs of the body and we anticipate this will help to develop new tests, new treatments and impact on healthcare. Executive summary Study aims: The PHOSP-COVID consortium aims are: i) to describe the holistic impact of long COVID on people that were hospitalised with COVID-19, ii) to identify the features associated either with good or poor recovery, iii) to investigate the underlying causes of long COVID, iv) to determine whether long COVID is altered by treatments given for the acute infection and v) to develop treatments for people with long COVID to improve recovery. Background: In the wake of the pandemic post-acute sequelae of COVID-19, known as long COVID, have emerged. Long COVID is a chronic illness in people experiencing ongoing symptoms and disability beyond four weeks after infection (NICE 2020). PHOSP-COVID ( PHOSP.org ) is a UK consortium established in the summer 2020 comprising of leading multi-disciplinary researchers and clinicians, with patient, public and voluntary sector involvement (PPI), working together to understand and improve long-term health outcomes for adults who were discharged from hospital following COVID-19. Methods: The PHOSP-COVID consortium includes 83 hospitals, 25+ universities, 10+ patient groups and charities, and 500+ researchers. We recruited adults discharged from hospital after COVID-19 between Feb 2020–March 2021 to three tiers of research: ‘Tier 1 which utilised use of routine health data, questionnaires, and a saliva sample for genetic testing; ‘Tier 2’ involving early (5 month) and later 12 month visits which included deep phenotyping with patient reported outcomes measures (PROMS) capturing physical symptoms, mental health, health related quality of life, and measures of cognitive impairment, device-measured 24h physical activity profiling, muscle strength, exercise capacity, frailty and organ impairment including clinical blood tests and lung function tests. A bioresource was collected sampling blood, urine, sputum and oral wash. For ‘Tier 3’ people from Tier 1 or Tier 2 were recalled for additional visits or procedures for example for more detailed immune tests and multi-organ magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). All participants were asked to consent to further follow-up for 25 years via linkage to their electronic healthcare records and to be re-contacted for further research. Cohort data are held in a Trusted Research Environment (TRE) and samples stored in a central biobank. Data and samples can be accessed upon request and subject to approvals from https://www.phosp.org/data-sample-request/ . Results: Recruitment across the four UK nations included 7935 participants (Tier 1: 5238, Tier 2: 2697). We have published several key findings which are summarised below. These can be found on the website - https://www.phosp.org/publications - and include publications in Lancet and Lancet family of journals, Nature family of journals, Science Immunology, AJRCCM, Thorax, European Respiratory Journal. The early key findings were that at 5 months after hospital discharge from COVID-19, only about 30% of people self-reported that they had fully recovered. The proportion was similar after 1 year with only marginal improvement from 5 months to 1 year. Participants were less likely to have recovered if female, aged 35- 65 years old, body mass index >30, or they had multiple long-term conditions prior to COVID-19 or required mechanical ventilation whilst hospitalised. We found that the treatments given for the acute infection such as corticosteroids did not affect the likelihood of recovery consistent with the 6-month follow-up of the REMAP-CAP study. Through unsupervised cluster analysis, we identified the severity of physical and mental health largely grouped together whereas ‘brain-fog’ can occur on its own. Those with the most severe health impairments had evidence of persistent inflammation reflected by an elevated c-reactive protein. Multi-organ, multi-modality MRI revealed changes in the brain, lungs and kidneys but no significant increase in cardiac or liver abnormalities compared to controls. Normal electrocardiogram reliably excluded cardiac MRI abnormalities. People with a higher burden of multi-organ injury were more likely to report poor physical and mental recovery. With specific co-morbid conditions people with diabetes, cardiovascular disease or cardiovascular risk factors or pre-existing airway diseases had worse symptoms and physical outcomes up to 12 months after hospital discharge with COVID-19. title: Editorial: Public health challenges in post-Soviet countries during and beyond COVID-19, volume II
abstract: On January 30, 2020, the WHO Director-General accepted the recommendation of the Emergency Committee and declared the novel coronavirus outbreak (2019-nCoV) a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC)(1). Post-Soviet countries (PSC) faced significant challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic. As for many other countries, the pandemic was the first experience of such magnitude for Ministries of Health (MoH) since the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. Therefore, many MoHs in the PSC lacked the necessary infrastructure, protocols, and staff to manage such events. However, while public health systems in many developing countries elsewhere are subpar, PSC inherited systems based on the Semashko model that were undergoing reforms to varying degrees (2). This factor proved critical to countries' capacity to respond to the pandemic, as public health emergency response systems had not been updated since Soviet times. These limitations are especially evident in the lack of progress in incorporating upto-date methodologies of disease surveillance and laboratory testing. As a result, the COVID-19 pandemic became a system shock that challenged the readiness of public health emergency response capacities. While it is clear that PSCs were not ready (as in many developed countries), it is not clear whether the MoHs in these countries have learned their lessons and strengthened their capacities to face the next pandemic.The COVID-19 pandemic had devastating impacts on public health, leading to the inaccessibility of health services for many people in need, catastrophic healthcare expenditures, and premature deaths. The countries experienced a shortage of facilities and medical professionals, a shortage that was particularly pronounced due to earlier reductions in hospital beds. Resources proved to be insufficient due to a severe shortage of essentials like medicines, diagnostic tests, and personal protective equipment, particularly during the peak period (3,4).Researchers from the region investigated aspects of public health systems such as a shift towards private healthcare. The example of Kazakhstan gives an interesting perspective for readiness as its healthcare system was based on the Soviet-era system, and the private healthcare sector was almost non-existenthttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/publichealth/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1608557/full (6). However, in the decade preceding the pandemic, healthcare shifted towards a higher number of private healthcare facilities. Thus, the pandemic required the government of Kazakhstan to mobilize both public and private healthcare providers to address the dramatic increase in patients. Although private hospitals were not originally adapted to manage large-scale infectious disease outbreaks, they adjusted by setting up COVID-19 units, at the cost of considerable business disruptions due to decreased patient flow and financial constraints.The pandemic exacerbated many prior challenges in the healthcare system of PSC, including issues of trust and violence against healthcare workers: up to 38% of healthcare professionals experience some form of violence in the workplace (7). The COVID-19 pandemic brought not only increased workloads and burnout, but a threat of violence from patients and family members (8)(9)(10). Moreover, the pandemic has eroded the societal respect traditionally given to healthcare workers (11): in Moldova, almost half of the violence aimed at healthcare workers primarily involved verbal threats; the COVID-19 pandemic increased concerns about workplace violencehttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/publichealth/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1560096/full. COVID-19 infection brought new attention to chronic diseases, including cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus. While these diseases traditionally affect older populations, their prevalence among younger populations is increasing (12). (13) forecast a rise in cardiovascular disease and stroke prevalence in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan. This is concerning, as patients with chronic diseases were at a higher risk of severe complications and death from COVID-19 (14)(15)(16).The pandemic's demographic effects were significant worldwide, though different countries reacted differently to lockdowns, declining birth rates, reduced in-person communication, fear of COVID-19, and other issues. ( 17) report no long-term effect on birthrate in Kazakhstan, which might suggest a limited effect of the pandemic on life. However, long-term studies on birthrate and reproductive health are needed, as some studies suggest that COVID-19 infection might have long-term effects on the reproductive system, including hormonal disturbances that can affect regularity of the menstrual cycle, ovulatory function, and receptivity of the endometrium (18). Data from United States suggests that the COVID-19 pandemic has worsened existing health disparities and disproportionately affected racial and ethnic minorities (19). As reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, segregated ethnic groups have experienced higher rates of infection, hospitalization, and death compared to other populations (20). These findings were corroborated by European studies (21,22), which report that people living in segregated, lowincome neighborhoods were affected by disproportionately higher rates of COVID-19 infections. One of the other vulnerable groups are older adults, particularly 65 and over, who were at the higher risk for severe complications and death from COVID-19 and thus requiring improved access to healthcare services for both acute and chronic conditions (23). A survey of 1,503 Lithuanians aged 65 and overhttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/publichealth/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1504049/full reports that the primary reasons for nonutilization of healthcare services included fear of COVID-19 infection for 1 in 6 respondents. These studies provide further support for the view that the COVID-19 pandemic had a significant effect on healthcare systems worldwide, limiting access to routine healthcare and exacerbating inequalities in access to healthcare (25).Health-related behaviors in older adults were also affected during and after the COVID-19 pandemic: in Lithuania, there was a decrease in physical activity, face-to-face communications, and an increase in remote communication in older adults in Lithuania. Factors like education, income, age, residence, and health status affected these outcomes, suggesting that a differential approach is needed for mitigating negative outcomes from the pandemichttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/publichealth/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1504193/full.While the WHO declared the end of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2023, populations across the world were reminded of dangers posed by fast spreading and deadly viruses. Public attention to emerging viruses was at all time high during and several years after the pandemic, but the challenges associated with managing a large epidemic are still potentially there. While thousands of research papers were dedicated to the COVID-19 pandemic, much lesser attention is given to lessons learned from the pandemic, or state of readiness in case of another worldwide outbreak of infectious disease.One of the significant challenges in PSC during the pandemic was undiagnosed infection. The potential undercount of overall cases has been estimated to be by 55-60% by official statistics (27), although managing the COVID-19 pandemic may have also decreased healthcare systems' ability to surveil and report other infectious diseases https . COVID-19 pandemic also brought new attention to hygiene among different population groups, including children (29,30): the majority of school children in Karaganda region, Kazakhstan, showed appropriate hand hygiene practices, though only one-fourth of the students washed hands after contact with a sick friend. Therefore, to reduce the spread of infectious disease among school children, public health interventions should focus on behavioral reinforcement in addition to education, including habit formation techniques and peer modelinghttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/publichealth/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1593579/full. Overall, studies from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic exposed gaps in the PSC public health capacity and pandemic preparedness, reflect on risks associated with health delivery services, violence against health workers, and population behavior, as well as the impact of COVID-19 on the intersection of chronic and infectious diseases.However, the studies were predominantly cross-sectional designs and data on long-term public health impacts or the persistent effects of the COVID-19 pandemic or comparison of health systems pre-and post-pandemic period are lacking. Globally, lessons from the pandemic have emphasized the need for comprehensive health policies that strengthen national health systems on the foundations of public health and universal health coverage, focusing on the management and prevention of both chronic and infectious diseases while maintaining a strong emphasis on population health behavior, especially among vulnerable populations. Countries should determine and expand national pandemic preparedness plans to prevent and respond to newly emerging infectious diseases.

title: Concordance and discordance between policymaker and family physician experiences of the COVID-19-driven rise of virtual care in Nova Scotia.
abstract: Abstract Aim: To describe and understand areas of concordance and discordance between the perceptions and experiences of family physicians and policymakers regarding the implementation and use of virtual care within the Nova Scotian primary care system. Background: COVID-19 brought rapid change to primary care delivery and accessibility. Virtual care rapidly expanded, facilitating primary care access amidst public health restrictions. Health systems leaders facilitated access to virtual care, developed and implemented guidelines, and created new billing codes. Providers integrated virtual care and operation changes into practice. Methods: Semi-structured interviews with family physicians (n = 20), policymakers (n = 9) and a family physician/policymaker (n = 1) were conducted to understand virtual care implementation and outcomes in Nova Scotia, Canada, identifying benefits and challenges. Findings: All participants discussed patient confidentiality concerns, overreliance potential, and virtual care to promote patient care access. Family physicians discussed provider privacy and burnout. Policymakers discussed virtual care increasing capacity for accepting new patients and challenges evaluating virtual care billing codes. Providers and policymakers shared concerns and policy directions for development and expansion of virtual care. As there is little research from policymaker perspectives on virtual care, reconciling these viewpoints is crucial for effectiveness and sustainability.
journal: Primary Health Care Research and Development

title: Protective Effect of COVID-19 Vaccination on Post-Infection Visuospatial Deficits.
abstract: OBJECTIVE COVID-19 has been associated with persistent cognitive deficits months after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Vaccination reduces severe disease, but its effect on post-infection cognition remains uncertain. We evaluated whether COVID-19 vaccination attenuates cognitive deficits after SARS-CoV-2. METHODS We assessed 237 adults with COVID-19 and 105 controls. Patients were grouped by vaccination status at infection (vaccinated n=87; unvaccinated n=150). The neuropsychological assessment covered language, visuospatial ability, visual memory, verbal memory, attention, executive functions, and working memory. Group differences were tested with Aligned Rank Transform ANOVA with Holm-corrected post hoc comparisons, adjusting for education. RESULTS Significant group differences were observed in visuospatial ability and visual memory, assessed with the Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test (Copy, Immediate and Delayed Recall) (all p < 0.001). The vaccinated group outperformed the unvaccinated group (p = 0.022) on visuospatial performance. The Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test Copy did not differ significantly among participants vaccinated with CoronaVac, AstraZeneca, or Pfizer. CONCLUSIONS The findings suggest that COVID-19 vaccination may mitigate post-infection visuospatial deficits, reinforcing the importance of immunization in preventing cognitive sequelae associated with the disease.

Group differences were tested with Aligned Rank Transform ANOVA with Holm-corrected post hoc comparisons, adjusting for education. RESULTS Significant group differences were observed in visuospatial ability and visual memory, assessed with the Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test (Copy, Immediate and Delayed Recall) (all p < 0.001).
