title: Social distancing under strategic uncertainty: The role of strategic sophistication in the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Abstract This study examines how individuals’ strategic sophistication shapes social distancing during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, when distancing was a costly protective decision under two sources of risk: the private risk of infection and strategic uncertainty about whether others would comply. We develop a weakest-link public goods game with private costs of social distancing, in which agents differ in their level- k depth of reasoning about others. The model predicts that the probability of distancing rises with the level- k type when baseline compliance is low. We test this prediction using large-scale, nationally representative survey data that include incentivized experiments to measure participants’ level- k types. We find that a one-level increase in level- k lowers the probability of leaving home daily by 1.6 percentage points in Singapore and is associated with a 3.4 percentage-point lower probability of maintaining or increasing outdoor activity in South Korea.

title: Serologic Testing for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus and SARS-CoV-2 Cross-Reactive Immune Responses, the Netherlands
abstract: Cross-reactive SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies could compromise the specificity of MERS-CoV serology, potentially leading to misclassification of infection history. SARS-CoV-2 exposure induced MERS-CoV antibodies primarily targeting the conserved S2 domain, with occasional neutralizing capacity. Combining MERS-CoV S1 binding with neutralization, however, limited the influence of SARS-CoV-2-induced cross-reactivity on MERS-CoV serology.

title: COVID 19 and fungal infection - A double disaster:a case series.
abstract: The recent Coronavirus pandemic in 2019 [COVID-19] was associated with an increased risk of opportunistic fungal co-infection. This case series presents 5 autopsy-confirmed fungal co-infections identified in patients who died following COVID-19. Among the notable findings were Fusarium-associated fungal myocarditis and human infection with Hormographiella, an extremely rare pathogen found in COVID-19. To the best of our knowledge, the latter represents the first reported fungal co-infection with this pathogen in COVID-19. We also report the first postmortem diagnosis of invasive pulmonary mucormycosis in COVID-19 in Sri Lanka, confirmed with culture as Rhizopus spp. Postmortem examination, histopathological analysis and fungal culture revealed fungal infections that had not been suspected clinically or had been only partially characterized, and provided the microbiological and pathological evidence necessary for establishing the cause of death These findings highlight the medicolegal importance of thorough autopsy examination in severe COVID-19, especially in situations where opportunistic fungal infection may have contributed to death.

title: Aerobic physical activity is associated with lower pneumonia and COVID-19 mortality in adults with cognitive impairment.
abstract: Cardiovascular disease and pneumonia are major causes of death in dementia, but cause-specific mortality has rarely been examined in clinically confirmed cognitive-impairment cohorts. In this nationwide retrospective cohort study, 116,563 individuals with clinically confirmed mild cognitive impairment or dementia in the Korean Dementia Relief Center registry (2016-2021) were linked to health screening and death registry data. Aerobic physical activity (APA) was quantified in metabolic-equivalent minutes per week (MET·min/week). Cox proportional hazards and Fine-Gray models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) and subdistribution HRs (sHRs). The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure controlled the false discovery rate (FDR) across 18 cause-specific comparisons. During 400,500 person-years of follow-up (mean, 3.4 years), 5022 participants (4.31%) died. Compared with inactivity, low, moderate, and high APA were associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR [95% CI], 0.728 [0.652-0.813], 0.704 [0.636-0.781], and 0.636 [0.590-0.687], respectively). High APA was associated with lower pneumonia mortality (sHR, 0.554; 95% CI, 0.437-0.702) and COVID-19 mortality (sHR, 0.520; 0.368-0.735). These point estimates were numerically lower than for ischemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disease (sHRs, 0.613 and 0.630). Pneumonia mortality was lower across all APA levels after FDR control (q ≤ 0.023). The E-value for the high APA-pneumonia association was 3.01. APA was associated with lower mortality even at modest activity levels, especially for pneumonia deaths. Achievable activity goals may therefore merit prospective evaluation as part of supportive care for adults with cognitive impairment. Because APA may also indicate preserved physiological reserve, these findings do not establish causality and require confirmation using repeated, objective activity measurements.

title: Long-term communication and swallowing disability in adults with persistent critical illness following COVID-19: A mixed-methods observational study.
abstract: Objectives To describe the lived experience of communication and swallowing disability in adults with persistent critical illness following COVID-19. Methods A mixed-methods study. Semi-structured interviews were conducted alongside patient-reported communication and swallowing outcome measures. Setting Participants were recruited from a registry-embedded COVID-Recovery study. All patients were eligible if they were ≥ 18 years, positive PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and had persistent critical illness. This was defined as admission to ICU for >10 consecutive days with invasive mechanical ventilation for at least 24 h. Main outcome measures Semi-structured interviews were used to explore communication and swallowing disability. Additional patient-reported outcomes were assessed with the Dysphagia Severity Rating Scale and the La Trobe Communication Questionnaire. General function outcomes were evaluated with the WHODAS 2.0, EQ-5D-5L, HADS, MoCA-Blind, IADL and IES-6. Findings Of the 113 participants followed up, 29/113 (26%) reported communication or swallowing disability, and of these 17/29 (59%) consented to semi-structured interviews. From the 16 participants who answered questions about communication function 100% self-reported difficulty in ≥1 communication domain, including expressive language 13/16 (81%), voice 13/16 (81%), receptive language 9/16 (56%) and speech 5/16 (31%). Although all participants were consuming an oral diet and most with nil texture restrictions (13/17,76%), many reported ongoing swallowing concerns regarding safety and efficiency. Impacts of these new disabilities were beyond physical function and impacted on their activities and participation. Recovery was unclear, prolonged and compounded by judgement from others. Participants navigated their own recovery journey and whilst some were well supported, others described critical healthcare gaps. Conclusions We identified approximately one quarter of people admitted to ICU for COVID-19 related critical illness with a length of stay of 10 days or more report ongoing communication and swallowing disability at 6 months. The impacts continued well beyond hospital discharge and highlight a need to specifically address swallowing and communication in recovery pathways. Implications for clinical practice Specific assessment of communication and swallowing function is essential for individuals who experience persistent critical illness.

title: Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and control measures on type 2 diabetes care among South Asians: the perspective of healthcare providers in British Columbia, Canada.
abstract: Background British Columbia is one of the most ethnically diverse provinces in Canada, with South Asians emerging as one of the fastest-growing ethnic minority groups, burdened by a high incidence of type 2 diabetes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many healthcare services shifted to virtual care to minimize infection transmission. Given the limited understanding of how primary care physicians in BC adapted their diabetes care approaches and the consequent impact on patient experience, this qualitative study aims to explore the effects of pandemic-related control measures on primary care diabetes services in BC from the perspectives of general practitioners, focusing particularly on their South Asian patients. Methods We conducted semi-structured interviews with ten primary care physicians serving large South Asian patient populations. Interviews explored the pandemic's effects on care delivery, provider adaptations, and consequences for South Asian patients with diabetes. Sessions were held in person or via Zoom/Teams and transcribed verbatim. Transcripts underwent thematic content analysis to identify recurring themes and insights regarding barriers, adaptations, and recommendations to improve diabetes care. Findings The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted diabetes care, shifting services to virtual care and interrupting routine monitoring. This transition impacted specific aspect of diabetes care that can best be provided in-person (e.g., foot examinations, blood pressure checks and lifestyle counselling). The pandemic compounded existing issues, e.g., cost, concerns with side effects, and medication compliance among South Asian patients. Physicians also observed a general rise in anxiety and depression during the pandemic among their patients. Older South Asian patients faced additional cultural, language, and digital barriers; physicians struggled to obtain timely Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) tests. For many patients, a significant reliance on pharmacists embedded within certain physician's clinics, ensured an uninterrupted access to diabetes medication and supplies. Conclusion The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted diabetes care, with some groups facing additional cultural, language, and digital barriers. Our findings highlight the need for primary care reforms: improved telemedicine and EMR infrastructure, and policies to support virtual care. Bridging the digital divide and implementing targeted supports are essential to minimize care disruption for vulnerable populations during future pandemics or similar crises and ensure equity.

title: Non-hospitalised Children & young people (CYP) with Long Covid (CLoCk) - COV-LT-0022
abstract: Plain English Summary Some children and young people (CYP) remain ill for a long time after infection with the COVID virus. They are said to have long COVID. There is no simple blood test or scan for long COVID. Early in the recent worldwide COVID outbreak (pandemic), no-one knew how common it is or how long it goes on for. We needed to know more about it if we want to treat it. Over 30,000 CYP aged 11-17 years agreed to take part in our research, half of whom we knew had a positive PCR test which showed they had been infected with the COVID virus. Initially, we were able to compare these participants with the half who didn’t test positive – so-called negative controls. Our research has shown that the risk factors for long COVID in CYP include female sex, older age, pre-existing diseases, pre-existing mental health problems, having an adult carer with long COVID and coming from an ethnic minority. Our results also helped the World Health Organisation come up with a working definition of long COVID in CYP, based on the problems CYP described as there is no blood test or scan to diagnose long COVID. Finally, we were able to show convincingly that most CYP with long COVID got better by 2 years. For some this took a long time, up to 2 years, but even among those CYP with multiple persisting problems, most got better. Sadly, a quarter still described persisting problems affecting their quality of life after 2 years. More research is needed to understand how best to support and treat CYP whose symptoms do not improve. Executive Summary Study Aims: The overall aim of our research was to describe and define long COVID in children and young people (CYP). Specifically, we aimed to:(1) Describe the clinical phenotype of long COVID symptomatology in test positive CYP, using test negative comparators;(2) Use these data to produce an operational definition of long COVID, necessary for any future epidemiological or interventional study; and (3) Use this definition to establish the prevalence and nature of long COVID in CYP to inform NHS services and health policy. We hypothesised that the type, prevalence and trajectory of symptoms in COVID positive CYP would differ significantly from the comparator group, allowing us to construct an operational definition of long COVID. Background: As early as March 2020, patient advocacy groups highlighted that survivors of SARS-CoV-2 were often left with persistent health issues, which soon extended to children and young people (CYP). By Autumn 2020, these ongoing health problems, termed 'long COVID' or Post COVID Condition, were also reported in CYP, but little was known about its diagnosis, prevalence, or treatment. There was no established definition or diagnostic test for long COVID, and it wasn’t captured in NHS datasets. title: Protein provision and associations with changes in skeletal and diaphragm muscle during COVID-19 critical illness.
abstract: Background During COVID-19 critical illness, both muscle mass and muscle strength decline. Protein provision is one of the factors influencing changes in muscle mass and may therefore also play a role in diaphragm atrophy. The aim of this study was to investigate whether protein provision is related to changes in skeletal muscle and diaphragm muscle mass and quality in critically ill COVID-19 patients during the first 30 days of ICU admission. We studied skeletal muscle area (SMA) and diaphragm volume (DV) as markers of muscle mass. As indicators of muscle quality, skeletal muscle density (SMD) and diaphragm density (DD) were studied. Methods This is a retrospective cohort study including adult critically ill COVID-19 patients who were mechanically ventilated for ≥48 hours and had at least two available computed tomography (CT) scans. SMA (cm 2 ) and DV (cm 3 ) were segmented, and quality (Hounsfield Units, HU) was assessed. Linear mixed-model analysis was performed to study the association between both average weight-based protein provision (g/kg /day) and average adequate or low protein provision (≥1.2 vs. Results A total of 93 patients with available data on skeletal muscle were included. Diaphragm data were available in a subgroup of 28 patients. Protein provision (g/kg/day) was not significantly related to changes in SMA, DV, SMD and DD. SMD decreased significantly over time (-0.3 HU per day, 95% CI -0.4 to -0.2, p Conclusion There was no clear relationship between the amount of protein administered and changes in SMA, DV, SMD and DD. Skeletal muscle quality decreased over time, but skeletal muscle mass, diaphragm volume and quality appeared to remain stable during the first 30 days of ICU admission.

title: Age and oxygen saturation predict cognitive performance in covid- 19 survivors at least two months after discharge
abstract: Abstract Background COVID19 is viral illness resulting in acute respiratory syndrome. The acute disease can be followed by persistent multisystemic sequelae and in particular neuropsychiatric ones. We asked what are the risk factors and physiological markers of cognitive performance in COVID-19 survivors. Methods We analysed real-world clinical data from 159 COVID-19 survivors aged 40 years or older who were assessed in an outpatient clinic at least two months after discharge. The main outcome variable was the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) total score. Predictor variables included demographics, anthropometric measures, pulmonary function, six-minute walk test measures, sit-to-stand performance and self-reported sleep quality. Exploratory factor analysis was used to reduce the dimensionality of the predictor sets. Linear regression following multiple imputation was used to identify predictors of cognitive performance. Results In the initial multivariate linear regression MoCA scores were predicted by age and a composite of oxygen-saturation measurements derived from the six-minute walk test assessment. No other predictor variable was significant. In a subsequent analysis we examined the effects of age, oxygen saturation (SpO2) and their interaction. All three predictors were significant. In particular, the effect of SpO2 on MoCA score was modulated by age, as cognitive performance in older individuals was more susceptible to decrements in SpO2 than younger individuals. Conclusion Lower oxygen saturation is associated with lower MoCA scores in older COVID-19 survivors, compared to younger adults. These findings may suggest that respiratory function is a therapeutic target for older COVID-19 survivors experiencing cognitive decline in the post-infectious period.

title: The Extracellular Matrix is Potentially a Key Regulator in Long COVID, Hypermobility Disorders, and Related Conditions
abstract: Long coronavirus disease (long COVID) and hypermobility disorders (e.g., hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) often share comorbidities, including mast cell activation syndrome, small fiber neuropathy, and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome. The relationship between long COVID and hypermobility disorders, as well as the extracellular matrix (ECM), has been reported, with evidence suggesting that ECM alterations may underlie these associations. The current hypothesis posits that ECM alterations may become partly self-perpetuating, with the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 spike protein as a possible initial trigger. The proposed mechanism involves interactions among the spike protein, integrins, latent transforming growth factor β, mast cells, interleukin-6, and matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9). Possible feedback loops, such as those between latent transforming growth factor β and a stiffened ECM, increased sympathetic activity and a pro-inflammatory state, insulin resistance and a pro-inflammatory state, inflammation and mast cell migration, and increased blood–brain barrier permeability via MMP-9 and inflammation, are highlighted. The impact of the modified ECM on the nervous system, as described through PIEZO and N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, is also discussed, alongside evidence for increased differentiation of T-helper 17 cells and their potentially disruptive effects on efferocytosis. This new hypothesis may have important implications for clinical practice and future research.

Possible feedback loops, such as those between latent transforming growth factor β and a stiffened ECM, increased sympathetic activity and a pro-inflammatory state, insulin resistance and a pro-inflammatory state, inflammation and mast cell migration, and increased blood–brain barrier permeability via MMP-9 and inflammation, are highlighted. The impact of the modified ECM on the nervous system, as described through PIEZO and N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, is also discussed, alongside evidence for increased differentiation of T-helper 17 cells and their potentially disruptive effects on efferocytosis. This new hypothesis may have important implications for clinical practice and future research.

title: Obstructive sleep apnea is frequent in patients with Long COVID fatigue but is not significantly associated with alterations of quality of life and cognition.
abstract: Neurologic manifestations of Long COVID, also called post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC), include fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, sleep disturbances, and headaches, which can be debilitating. Since these symptoms overlap with those of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), we sought to determine the prevalence of OSA in the population of a Neuro-COVID-19 clinic. We performed home sleep testing in 100 consecutive patients with Long COVID and no prior history of OSA who reported fatigue after an episode of COVID-19 not requiring hospitalization. The average age was 46.4 years and 70% of patients were female. OSA was present in 53% of patients, including 33% with mild OSA (apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) 5-14.9) and 20% with moderate to severe OSA (AHI ≥ 15). Male sex, higher age, and body mass index were significantly associated with OSA. However, there were no significant differences in other comorbidities, Long COVID symptom burden, quality of life measures (QoL), and objective cognitive function test results between groups. Additionally, multiple linear regression models demonstrated that neither AHI nor mean desaturation nadir were significant predictors of QoL or cognitive function. Although OSA is nearly twice as prevalent among our study participants compared to the general adult population of the US, it was not significantly associated with Long COVID symptoms, alteration of QoL, or objective cognitive dysfunction. However, 20% of patients were diagnosed with moderate to severe OSA, a clinically significant finding that warrants intervention to prevent irreversible cardiopulmonary complications.

title: Crystal structures of the N-terminal and C-terminal domains of the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein.
abstract: The nucleocapsid (N) protein of Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) functions in viral RNA binding, genome packaging and ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assembly. Crystal structures were determined of the N-terminal domain (NTD) from crystals grown at pH 8.0 to a resolution of 1.94 Å and of the C-terminal domain (CTD) from crystals grown at pH 5.0 and 8.5 to resolutions of 1.59 and 1.30 Å, respectively. The NTD adopts the canonical coronavirus NTD fold and contains a positively charged cleft corresponding to a previously proposed RNA-binding region. Comparison of the apo NTD structure determined in this study with a previously reported RNA-bound NTD structure revealed local differences in the side-chain conformations of RNA-contacting residues, including Thr49, Arg88, Arg92, Arg107, Tyr109 and Tyr111, whereas the overall domain fold remained essentially unchanged. These observations suggest that RNA binding may be accommodated by local side-chain rearrangements within a pre-existing positively charged cleft rather than by a large-scale conformational change. The CTD forms a domain-swapped dimer mediated by β-hairpins, with a positively charged groove extending across the dimer interface. Superposition of the two CTD structures yielded a root-mean-square deviation (r.m.s.d.) of 0.129 Å, and 11 intersubunit hydrogen bonds were observed at the dimer interface in each structure, indicating that the dimer architecture is conserved under the crystallization conditions examined. Together, these structures provide a framework for further investigation of NTD-RNA recognition, the possible role of the CTD positively charged groove in nucleic acid interactions and N-protein assembly.

title: Urotensin II: A Key Role in Hormonal and Inflammatory Cytokine Regulation in COVID-19 Patients.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic exhibits a wide spectrum of severities and pathophysiological mechanisms. The virus targets angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors, disrupting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) balance, which may explain various symptoms and risk factors. Fibrosis of the small airways is pivotal in the emergence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Understanding these complex pathophysiological mechanisms is crucial for developing effective treatments and personalized approaches for COVID-19 patients. The present study is aimed at analyzing the concentrations of the clinical and laboratory parameters-such as hematological, biochemical, serological, angiotensin II (ANG II), endothelin-1 (ET-1), urotensin II (UII), and cortisol parameters-in patients with SARS-CoV-2 and evaluating the elevation of these parameters related to the pathogenicity. The study included two distinct groups: a healthy control group (n = 25) and a COVID-19 patient group (n = 75) during the period from August 2021 to January 2022. Cytokine levels were evaluated using commercially available enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. The comparative analysis revealed that severe cases of COVID-19 have a significant elevation in the concentrations of hematological, biochemical, serological, and hormonal levels such as ANG II, ET-1, UII, and cortisol, as well as a substantial decline in the concentration of LYM%, in comparison with mild cases of COVID-19 and the control groups. Based on these findings, we concluded that ET-1, ANG II, and UII may be associated with COVID-19 pathophysiology and are linked to endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and thrombosis.

title: Prevalence of alpha-synuclein seeding activity in the Olfactory Mucosa following SARS-CoV-2 infection: results from a pilot study.
abstract: Olfactory dysfunction (OD) is a hallmark of SARS-CoV-2-infection where it is believed to result from neuroinflammation induced by viral invasion via the olfactory mucosa (OM). Hyposmia also affects the majority of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) where it is caused by α-synuclein (aSyn) pathology in the olfactory system, and aSyn-seeding-activity can be detected in the OM using aSyn-seeding-amplification-assays (aSyn-SAA). The present pilot study aimed to investigate whether SARS-CoV-2-infection induces local aSyn-misfolding and -aggregation in OM samples using aSyn-SAA. We conducted an observational study including PD patients (n = 51), individuals with a history of documented symptomatic SARS-CoV-2-infection (post-COVID; n = 95), and healthy controls (HC; n = 42). Post-COVID-participants were stratified based on persistent OD (COVID+OD; n = 42) or normal olfaction (COVID-OD; n = 53) using Sniffin'-Sticks-Identification (SSI) and -Discrimination (SSD) tests. OM samples were obtained by ENT specialists and analyzed by aSyn-SAA at the University of Verona. Clinical phenotyping included MDS-UPDRS, MoCA, and the Innsbruck-RBD-Inventory. OM-SAA positivity rates were significantly different between PD and both post-COVID-participants and HCs (80.4% vs 24.2% vs 11.9%; p < 0.001). Within the post-COVID-group, positivity rates were higher in COVID+OD vs COVID-OD (35.7% vs 15.1%; p = 0.030), and COVID+OD differed from HC (p = 0.030), while COVID-OD did not (p = 0.65). Among post-COVID-participants, aSyn-SAA positivity was associated with lower SSI (p = 0.007) and SSD (p < 0.001) scores, but not with MDS-UPDRS, MoCA, or RBD measures. OM-SAA-positivity was enriched among individuals with persistent post-COVID-OD and correlated with olfactory impairment. These findings support the hypothesis that neuroinflammation following SARS-COV-2-infection might promote local aSyn-aggregation. The biological and prognostic relevance of OM-SAA positivity is unknown and needs further prospective investigation.

title: High-Frequency Enhancement and Dual-Model Ensemble for Language-Guided COVID-19 Pneumonia Lesion Segmentation.
abstract: Accurate segmentation of COVID-19 pneumonia lesions in chest X-ray (CXR) images is critical for disease quantification and clinical decision-making. However, existing methods suffer from blurred lesion boundaries, missed detection of tiny lesions, and limited generalization performance. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a language-guided multimodal medical image segmentation method integrating high-frequency enhancement and a dual-model ensemble. The method is developed along three dimensions: frequency-domain detail enhancement, spatial alignment optimization, and dual-model ensemble. First, a frequency-domain decomposition-based high-frequency enhancement module is designed to mitigate detail attenuation caused by encoder downsampling. Second, a two-dimensional (2D) spatial position encoding module is introduced to improve the spatial alignment between text descriptions and visual regions. Third, a dual-model ensemble architecture with differentiated frequency-domain masks is constructed to address the performance ceiling of individual models. Finally, experiments on two public datasets with different imaging modalities and data characteristics demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing single-modal and multimodal baseline methods and achieves competitive performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches, verifying the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework. On the QaTa-COV19 dataset, the Dice coefficient reaches 91.85% and the mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) reaches 84.98%. On the multi-institutional MosMedData+ dataset, the Dice coefficient reaches 78.48% and the mIoU reaches 64.66%. The proposed method provides effective technical support for clinical diagnosis and follow-up assessment of pneumonia.

On the multi-institutional MosMedData+ dataset, the Dice coefficient reaches 78.48% and the mIoU reaches 64.66%. The proposed method provides effective technical support for clinical diagnosis and follow-up assessment of pneumonia.

title: Immunogenicity, Safety, and Clinical Outcomes Following Homologous and Heterologous SARS-CoV-2 Vaccination Regimens in Patients with Axial Spondyloarthritis and Psoriatic Arthritis: A Prospective Observational Study from the SAFER Cohort
abstract: Background/Objectives: Patients with spondyloarthritis (SpA) frequently receive immunomodulatory therapies that may influence vaccine-induced immune responses. However, evidence comparing the immunogenicity, safety, and clinical outcomes following homologous and heterologous SARS-CoV-2 vaccination regimens in axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) and psoriatic arthritis (PsA) remains limited. Methods: This observational study was conducted within the Brazilian multicenter SAFER cohort and included adults with axSpA or PsA who received three doses of SARS-CoV-2 vaccines through the Brazilian National Immunization Program. The primary outcome was humoral immunogenicity, assessed by anti-receptor-binding domain (anti-RBD) IgG geometric mean titers (GMTs). Clinical outcomes, disease activity, and safety were evaluated throughout follow-up. Results: Ninety patients (axSpA = 69; PsA = 21) were included. Antibody titers increased progressively after vaccination, with GMTs rising from 6.70 BAU/mL at baseline to 907.72 BAU/mL after the additional dose. Humoral responses were comparable between axSpA and PsA throughout follow-up. Participants with previous SARS-CoV-2 exposure consistently exhibited higher antibody responses than infection-naïve individuals. Although ChAdOx1-S elicited stronger early humoral responses than CoronaVac, heterologous regimens incorporating a BNT162b2 additional dose produced the highest post-additional-dose antibody concentrations. Serological response rates reached 100% after the additional dose, irrespective of disease subtype or vaccination regimen. Biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs), including TNF inhibitors, were not significantly associated with reduced antibody responses. Only four COVID-19 cases occurred during follow-up, with no hospitalizations or deaths. Disease activity remained stable, and adverse events were predominantly mild and self-limited. Conclusions: SARS-CoV-2 vaccination was safe and highly immunogenic in patients with axSpA and PsA, without compromising disease activity control. Heterologous vaccination regimens incorporating a BNT162b2 additional dose elicited the strongest humoral immune responses. These findings provide prospective real-world evidence supporting optimized additional-dose strategies and may inform future vaccination approaches for patients with SpA.

title: Adverse Birth Outcomes Associated With SARS-CoV-2 Infection Among Pregnant Women With and Without HIV: A Longitudinal Cohort Study.
abstract: Background COVID-19 and HIV infection are independently associated with increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. However, there is limited evidence on the effect of SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly among women living with HIV (WLWH). Setting Two antenatal clinics in southern Malawi (2018-2022). Methods We conducted a prospective cohort study of singleton pregnancies enrolled at 20-36 weeks gestation. SARS-CoV-2 infection was determined through serologic testing at enrollment and delivery. Participants were enrolled based on HIV status and viral suppression: (1) WLWH with detectable viral load (VL), (2) WLWH with undetectable VL, and (3) HIV-negative women. We used a multivariable logistic regression with adjustment for confounding to evaluate the effect of SARS-CoV-2 alone or in combination with HIV infection on the following adverse birth outcomes: low birth weight (LBW), preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age (SGA), and stillbirth or early neonatal death. Results Among 905 pregnant women, 29% tested positive for SARS-CoV-2, 87% of infections were mild or asymptomatic. Overall, SARS-CoV-2 infection was significantly associated with SGA births (adjusted OR [aOR]: 1.49, 95% CI: 1.03 to 2.13) but not associated with other adverse outcomes. Among WLWH, SARS-CoV-2 was significantly associated with increased odds of LBW (aOR: 2.07, 1.10 to 3.91) and SGA births (aOR: 1.73, 1.01 to 2.91). The effect of SARS-CoV-2 infection among WLWH did not differ based on VL. Conclusions SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy was associated with adverse birth outcomes, particularly among WLWH. These findings underscore the need for integrated antenatal care and targeted infection prevention strategies for pregnant women with HIV in high-burden settings.

title: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2)
abstract: Abstract This chapter reviews the scientific, operational, and regulatory factors that enabled the accelerated development, evaluation, and deployment of safe and effective vaccines during the global COVID-19 pandemic. It sets the historical underpinnings of foundational science that were necessary to enable the rapid understanding of a novel pathogen and its vulnerabilities. It further traces the origins of rapid vaccine response, contextualizes decades of prior basic research in virology and immunology, and highlights advances in platform technologies and antigen design. Multiple vaccine platforms are compared for their technological features and impact. This narrative also details how resources were mobilized, clinical trial networks repurposed, and regulatory frameworks evolved to shepherd the global community out of a public health crisis. This chapter concludes with a discussion of how COVID-19 has transitioned from a pandemic to endemic disease, why vaccine updates are needed to keep pace with SARS-CoV-2 evolution, and what enduring lessons have been gained for future public health emergencies.

title: Authentic E-Learning in Higher Education in the Post-COVID-19 Era: A Narrative Review
abstract: This narrative review examines the state of authentic e-learning in higher education in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, with particular attention paid to social work education in South Africa. It assesses whether the rapid move to online and blended learning has progressed beyond emergency remote teaching towards more meaningful, student-centred approaches. The review draws on peer-reviewed studies published between 2019 and 2024, identified through purposive and hand searches of Google Scholar, EBSCOhost and Sabinet using terms related to authentic learning, e-learning and post-COVID-19 higher education. Sources were selected for their relevance to the review’s guiding questions rather than through an exhaustive, protocol-driven search and read critically. The literature was organised thematically into three broad foci: (1) the benefits of authentic e-learning in higher education; (2) the challenges of implementing authentic e-learning in higher education; and (3) implications for rethinking social work education in line with the elements of authentic e-learning. The review indicates that authentic e-learning, grounded in real-world tasks, collaboration, reflection and interdisciplinary engagement, can enhance the quality, inclusivity and relevance of social work education, with reported benefits including flexibility, inclusivity and opportunities for international collaboration. Persistent challenges include the digital divide, personal and institutional constraints, limitations of learning management systems, and academic dishonesty. As a narrative rather than systematic review, this account is illustrative rather than exhaustive: its South African and social-work-specific focus, its reliance on three databases, and its inclusion of mostly small-scale, short-term primary studies mean that the themes identified should be read as indicative patterns in the literature rather than a comprehensive or generalisable evidence base. Recommendations for social work education include expanding broadband access, providing ongoing digital training, establishing clear institutional policies, and adopting agile, problem-based learning approaches. Building on, but distinct from the proposals advanced in the reviewed studies, this paper closes with a set of recommendations authored by the review team.

title: Impact of Covid-19 Pandemic on Nigerian Capital Market: The Imperative of Testing the Efficacy of Efficient Market Hypothesis
abstract: In this paper we reviewed the efficacy of Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH) on the outbreak of Covid-19 on Nigerian Capital Market. The EMH is a theory based on informational efficiency by the capital markets owing to their quick and instantaneous incorporation of new information. The study tested the market in two parameters: to confirm the randomness (efficiency of the market) using run-test, and to confirm the effect of Covid-19 protocols on some economic fundamentals using regression analysis. The result of the run-test of the daily Nigerian capital market data (April, 2020 to July 2020) revealed randomness within the period under review. The regression analysis however revealed significant relationship between the markets and some economic fundamental indicators (inflation and international price of crude oil) of the economy. The paper concluded that the Nigerian Capital Markets revealed randomness signifying a weak form of EMH as news about the Corona Virus was incorporated slowly but not instantaneously during the period under review, and hence, the pandemic did affect the market. The study also posited that EMH can be tested and validated not only from economic or finance point of view but also from public health view of the outbreak of Corona Virus. The paper recommended that policy makers in the country should devise a proper hedging mechanism to be put in place to mitigate any unforeseen negative market reactions in future as a result of any health pandemic.

title: A yeast surface display platform for oral delivery of a SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain dimer inducing mucosal and systemic immunity
abstract: The development of scalable and stable antigen delivery systems remains a central challenge in vaccine biotechnology, particularly for oral immunization targeting mucosal immunity. Here, we report a yeast surface display (YSD)-based platform for the oral delivery of a SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD) dimer. A head-to-tail tandem RBD was genetically fused to the Aga2p subunit and anchored to the cell wall of Saccharomyces cerevisiae via the Aga1p-Aga2p system, generating the YSD-RBD-dimer construct. Flow cytometry confirmed clear surface expression, with 51.1% dual-positive cells recognizing both HA-tag and RBD epitopes. Under simulated gastric conditions (pH 1.2), the antibody-binding signal associated with surface-displayed RBD-dimer showed 97.57% retention after 2 h, indicating preservation of antibody-accessible RBD-associated epitopes. In vivo fluorescence tracking revealed gastrointestinal transit with signals peaking in Peyer's patches at 6 h and mesenteric lymph nodes at 12 h. Oral immunization elicited both systemic and mucosal immune responses, characterized by elevated serum anti-RBD IgG and fecal secretory IgA. Notably, vaccine-induced sera substantially inhibited RBD-ACE2 binding in a cell-based assay, with an inhibition rate of 81.6% ± 6.4%. Antigen-specific lymphocyte proliferation and transcriptional analysis revealed a mixed Th1- and Th2-associated response, with greater induction of IFN-γ and T-bet than of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and GATA-3. No apparent systemic toxicity or histopathological abnormalities were observed, supporting the preliminary safety of the platform. Collectively, this study supports the feasibility of a scalable yeast surface display-based platform for oral delivery of protein antigens and induction of coordinated systemic and mucosal immune responses.

title: Understanding cognitive function in post-COVID-19 condition with fatigue: an interdisciplinary multimodal investigation
abstract: Lingering cognitive symptoms of post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) continue to challenge our understanding, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary research. We investigated whether individuals with PCC and fatigue differ from matched controls across neurocognitive, neuroimaging, and immunological measures, integrating these findings with qualitative phenomenological analyses through multimodal cross-analysis. Individuals with PCC and clinically significant fatigue (n=34), and age-, sex-, and education-matched controls recovered from COVID-19 without PCC (n=37) were included. Assessments encompassed physician evaluation, neuropsychological and functional tests, structural and functional MRI, immunological tests, and qualitative phenomenological analysis of interviews. Data were analyzed using established methods and an interdisciplinary cross-analysis to examine persistent cognitive symptoms in PCC. Group comparisons revealed subtle differences between individuals with PCC and controls, while neurocognitive performance and immunological markers remained within normative ranges. Modest differences in white matter, myelin related, and global brain measures were observed, alongside differences in associations between network connectivity and neurocognitive performance across groups, suggesting reduced network resilience rather than domain specific deficits. This pattern resonated with qualitative phenomenological findings: altered experiences of concentrating and difficulties to execute decisions and actions, despite preserved performance on standard neurocognitive tests. These findings suggest that cognitive symptoms in post-COVID-19 fatigue are associated with subtle neurobiological alterations not captured by standard cognitive assessments. In this highly fatigued sample, converging neuroimaging, neurocognitive and immunological findings point toward reduced network efficiency rather than overt cognitive impairment. Qualitative phenomenological analysis further highlighted altered modes of being in the world characterized by increased cognitive effort and difficulties executing decisions and actions.

title: Multifactorial biomarker profiles in fatigued and non-fatigued post-COVID-19 patients: insights from a one-year follow-up.
abstract: To compare blood biomarkers across SARS-CoV-2 fatigue, non-fatigue, and control groups; assessed longitudinal biomarker changes; and identified genetic associations and biomarkers linked to post-COVID-19 fatigue. This longitudinal observational study followed individuals with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection over a one-year period, stratifying them into fatigue (n = 27) and non-fatigue (n = 13) groups based on the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS). These groups were cross-sectionally compared with a non-infected control cohort (n = 27). Blood samples were collected at four time points to assess cytokines, hematological and biochemical markers, inflammatory indices, and matrix metalloproteinases. Selected functional polymorphisms were genotyped using PCR-RFLP. Group comparisons were conducted using generalized estimating equations, and genetic associations were evaluated using odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals. At baseline, fatigued post-COVID participants had higher IL-6 (2.70 vs. 1.68 pg/mL, p < 0.001), IL-8 (6.09 vs. 3.68 pg/mL, p = 0.024), and hs-CRP (6.61 vs. 1.06 mg/L, p < 0.001) than controls. Across follow-up, the fatigued group showed higher IL-6 (mean difference [MD] 1.27 pg/mL, p = 0.009), IL-8 (MD 1.98 pg/mL, p = 0.017), and hs-CRP (MD 4.16 mg/L, p < 0.001) than the non-fatigued group. In exploratory genotype analyses, fatigue was associated with COMT rs4680 (OR 13.85, 95% CI 2.74-69.91), NR3C1 rs41423247 (OR 3.76, 95% CI 1.04-13.69), and MMP9 rs3918242 (OR 0.20, 95% CI 0.06-0.67). Hs-CRP was significantly associated with FSS score (B = 0.12, 95% CI 0.02-0.21; p = 0.014). Post-COVID fatigue was associated with persistent inflammation and genetic variation, supporting a multifactorial biological basis and highlighting hs-CRP as a potential marker requiring further validation.

title: Hemorheological optimization via isovolemic hemodilution in COVID-19 ARDS under chronic environmental hypoxia: A pilot proof-of-concept study.
abstract: Chronic environmental hypoxia induces compensatory secondary erythrocytosis and elevated whole-blood viscosity, which may aggravate microvascular thromboinflammation in severe COVID-19 acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). We evaluated the feasibility, safety, and exploratory outcomes of isovolemic hemodilution (IVHD) in high-altitude COVID-19 ARDS. Retrospective cohort study of 30 consecutive adult lifelong high-altitude residents (elevation 3,640 m) admitted to the ICU with severe COVID-19 ARDS on invasive mechanical ventilation. Seven patients underwent clinician-selected IVHD (controlled phlebotomy of 0.5-2.0 L with isovolemic crystalloid replacement over 6-12 hours), while 23 received conventional ICU management. Baseline illness severity scores (APACHE II, PaO2) were comparable. Admission hematocrit was 59% (55-66) in the IVHD group versus 52% (36-68) in conventional controls (p=0.065). IVHD achieved rapid hemorheological decompression at 72 hours, reducing hematocrit to 38% (32-46, p=0.015) and hemoglobin to 11 g/dL (10-15, p=0.015). ICU survival was 71.4% (5/7) in the IVHD cohort versus 8.7% (2/23) in conventional controls (Fisher's exact p=0.003; crude odds ratio 26.25, 95% CI 2.9-234.3). No procedural adverse events occurred. Rapid hemorheological optimization via IVHD was feasible, safe, and associated with an exploratory survival signal in high-altitude COVID-19 ARDS, providing a physiological rationale for prospective randomized trials.

title: Feasibility, Accuracy, and Acceptability of Self-Collected Dried Blood Spots for Hepatitis C Virus, Hepatitis B Virus, and SARS-CoV-2 Testing.
abstract: Screening, diagnosis, and treatment for hepatitis C and hepatitis B can be limited due to challenges in accessing in-person health care. This study explored the alternative method of dried blood spot (DBS) collection, specifically through mail-based self-collection. A total of 388 patients were recruited by phone from the Toronto Centre for Liver Disease and the Toronto Western Family Health Team, who were seropositive for hepatitis C virus (HCV), hepatitis B virus, and/or SARS-CoV-2 or had unknown serostatus. Participants were mailed a collection kit, paper instructions/QR code for video instructions, demographic/acceptability questionnaires, a return envelope, and laboratory requisition. DBS cards and phlebotomy were tested for hepatitis B surface antigen, HCV antibody, and SARS-CoV-2 antibody. DBS results were compared against conventional phlebotomy as the gold standard. Of the 388 recruited participants, 110 completed the study by returning their DBS cards and completing conventional phlebotomy and questionnaires. For hepatitis B surface antigen, self-collection DBS testing showed 100% sensitivity and specificity, with 31 true positives and 79 true negatives. For HCV antibody, self-collection DBS testing showed 96.2% (25/26) sensitivity and 96.4% specificity (81/84), with 25 true positives, 81 true negatives, 3 false positives, and 1 false negative. SARS-CoV-2 testing also showed 100% sensitivity and specificity, with 108 true positives and 2 true negatives. Acceptability was high with 78.3% (101/129) participants rating the process easy or very easy. Mail-based self-collected DBS enables remote testing by allowing nonmedically trained individuals to reliably collect their own samples. High concordance and acceptability indicate that this method is viable for addressing health care access challenges, particularly in populations motivated to seek testing.

title: Minimised SARS-CoV-2 transmission during Tokyo 2020 Olympic and Paralympic Games: insights from enhanced integrated surveillance, Japan, July to September 2021
abstract: BACKGROUND Amid the COVID-19 pandemic, stringent public health measures were taken during the Tokyo 2020 Olympic and Paralympic Games (Tokyo 2020). AIM We describe SARS-CoV-2 transmission among Games participants and in-person contributors (GPIPC)s. METHODS Tokyo 2020-related SARS-CoV-2 infection cases were individuals linked to the event, testing positive for the virus between 1 July−19 September 2021, reported to the Tokyo Metropolitan Government. Attack rates among athletes and team officials were determined. Enhanced case-based surveillance integrating genomic sequencing data supported viral spread investigations among various GPIPC groups. RESULTS A total 804 cases (median age: 35 years, interquartile range (IQR): 27–45; 194 female/610 male) were reported. Among athletes and team officials, attack rates were 0.6% (65/11,400) in Olympic Games and 0.6% (30/4,800) in Paralympic Games. These 95 infections concerned mainly overseas travellers (n = 92), 85 of whom were diagnosed within 14 days of arrival in Japan. Among the 804 cases, whole-genome sequencing data were obtained for 304 (median age: 38 years, IQR: 29–47; 67 female/237 male) with sufficient viral load (as indicated by RT-PCR Cq ≤ 32), including 79% (75/95) of athletes and team officials cases, 74% (131/176) of Games’ organisers and media cases, and ˂ 20% (98/533) of remaining cases. Delta variants dominated (94%; 285/304), with domestic (AY.29 lineage) Delta strains prominent among Delta-variant-affected resident cases (96%; 104/108) and Games’ organisers and media cases diagnosed ≥ 15 days after entering Japan (97%; 63/65). Overseas Delta strains mostly affected travellers within 14 days of entry, particularly athletes and team officials (97%; 66/68) and Games’ organisers and media (29/34). CONCLUSION Multilayered-risk-reduction measures likely minimised SARS-CoV-2 transmission to athletes.

CONCLUSION Multilayered-risk-reduction measures likely minimised SARS-CoV-2 transmission to athletes.

title: New Nurse Graduate Readiness for Medication Administration Within the Context of the COVID-19 Pandemic.
abstract: Medication administration (MA) has significant implications for patient safety. This qualitative descriptive study, using semistructured interviews, explored the MA experiences of nine newly graduated registered nurses (NGRNs) whose undergraduate studies were primarily undertaken during the pandemic. Two themes were identified: work readiness and transitioning. NGRNs felt that pandemic restrictions, including condensed content delivery and delayed clinical placements, led to curriculum concerns and impeded MA learning. NGRNs valued structured hospital graduate programs and the support received from colleagues and preceptors. Longitudinal studies of the career impact of nurses whose education was disrupted during the pandemic are recommended.

title: Phase-Specific Changes in Korean Adolescents' Health Behaviors and Mental Health Across COVID-19 School Closure and Reopening.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted school routines, but health changes during school reopening remain unclear. This study examined phase-specific changes in health behaviors and mental health among Korean adolescents. Nationally representative Korea Youth Risk Behavior Survey data (2018-2024) were analyzed across pre-pandemic, pandemic, transition, and post-pandemic phases. Outcomes included health risk behaviors, diet and physical activity, obesity, and mental health indicators. Weighted prevalence estimates and logistic regression models were used. The analytic sample included 376,066 adolescents (51.8% boys). Current smoking declined from 6.4% (95% CI, 6.1-6.7) pre-pandemic to 3.8% (3.6-4.0) post-pandemic, whereas breakfast skipping increased from 34.5% (34.0-34.9) to 41.6% (41.1-42.0). Although moderate-to-vigorous physical activity exceeded its pre-pandemic level post-pandemic, obesity prevalence increased from 10.9% (10.7-11.2) to 12.2% (11.9-12.5). Suicidal ideation decreased during the pandemic but peaked at 14.0% (13.6-14.5) during transition. During reopening, schools should strengthen healthy meal and physical activity programs, sustain substance-use prevention, and ensure equitable access to mental health screening and referral. Recovery was uneven across health domains, identifying school reopening as a critical prevention window requiring sustained, phase-specific intervention.

title: Evaluation of Ferritin Levels in individuals with COVID-19: A Laboratory-Based Observational Research Investigation
abstract: COVID-19 has emerged as a major public health concern because of its rapid transmission and the high mortality risk associated with severe cases. Although considerable research has been conducted, the disease's pathophysiological processes and diagnostic indicators still require further investigation. Early detection, continuous patient monitoring, and appropriate therapeutic interventions are essential for improving clinical outcomes and reducing mortality. Serum ferritin has attracted attention as a potential indicator of inflammation and disease severity in patients with COVID-19. This study aimed to determine serum ferritin levels in patients with confirmed COVID-19 and explore their potential association with disease severity. A study was conducted at the Yafran Pathology Center and the Analysis Laboratory in the Andalusia District. We analyzed blood samples from patients with confirmed COVID-19 according to standard laboratory procedures. Serum ferritin concentrations were measured using the Integra 400 Plus analyzer. A total of 293 patients, including males and females, were enrolled in the study. Participants were classified into five age categories: 0–17 years, 18–34 years, 35–49 years, 50–64 years, and 65 years or older. Increased serum ferritin concentrations may be associated with greater severity of COVID-19. Ferritin could therefore be a useful potential biomarker for evaluating disease severity and supporting clinical decision-making. However, further statistical analysis is needed to determine the significance of this relationship and assess its predictive value.

title: Divergent Shifts in Paediatric Emergency Care Before, During, and After the COVID-19 Pandemic: An Interrupted Time Series Analysis
abstract: Abstract Background The COVID-19 pandemic resulted in the implementation of various public health measures that significantly disrupted healthcare utilization. This study examines the impact of the pandemic on paediatric emergency department (ED) visit trends in Ontario, Canada. Methods We performed interrupted time series analysis using administrative health data for ED visits reported across 206 EDs in Ontario from April 2011 to May 2023 (13,103,307 visits). Using negative binomial regression, we analyzed monthly trends in ED visits across four age groups (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, and 15–17 years). ED visits were categorized as urgent or non-urgent based on the Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS). Results Prior to pandemic onset, urgent ED visits increased at a rate of 0.22% per month, while non-urgent visits declined by 0.35% per month. The immediate reduction in visits was most severe in the 0–4 age group (–58.7%) and least severe in the 15–17 age group (–45.2%). Overall, no significant differences existed in the rate of recovery between urgent and non-urgent visits. Across the four age groups, the 0–4 age group demonstrated the steepest post-pandemic recovery in urgent visits (+ 3.32% per month). Conclusion The pandemic caused an unprecedented decline in pediatric ED utilization. While total volumes have largely recovered by the end of the pandemic, the shift towards a larger proportion of urgent visits has intensified. These findings suggest a change in how paediatric patients use EDs, highlighting the need for healthcare systems to adapt to this shift.

title: Data-driven forecasting of Flu, RSV, and COVID-19 related outcomes in the United States and Canada via Hankel dynamic mode decomposition.
abstract: The (large) season-to-season variability and limited dynamical history make the forecasting of infectious diseases a challenging problem. Here, we examine the extent to which advances in data-driven dynamical modeling can provide accurate predictions by benchmarking the performance of one such method, Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), on the 2024-2025 influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and COVID-19 seasons in the United States and Canada. Using Hankel-DMD, we generated weekly forecasts that were submitted to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC) FluSight Forecast Hub and the University of Guelph's AI4CastingHub. Across both Hubs, we find that Hankel-DMD can provide high quality forecasts at the beginning and end of the season, but forecasts in the middle of the season suffer from significant overestimation of the season peak. This leads to worse than baseline performance on FluSight Forecast Hub, when submissions are evaluated across the entire season. Hankel-DMD is found to be the best among a small number of models that submitted enough forecasts against which to compare for forecasting influenza, RSV, and COVID-19 in Canada. As this was the first active year of AI4CastingHub, this suggests that Hankel-DMD may be especially useful when expertise is lacking for predicting infectious dynamics in new regions. To study how Hankel-DMD can be better equipped to provide accurate forecasts during the season peak, we explored whether DMD with memory, a recently developed approach for applying DMD to non-stationary dynamical systems, provides significant improvements. Retrospective analysis using DMD with memory shows promise in reducing overestimation during season peak, but the extent to which its optimal use can be achieved in a live forecasting setting remains to be seen. Collectively, our results demonstrate that Hankel-DMD has potential as an efficient and interpretable method for the forecasting of infectious diseases, while also highlighting a number of remaining methodological challenges which future work should aim to address.

title: Treatment Success in Adults With Newly Diagnosed Type 2 Diabetes During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Single-Center Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Abstract Background The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted diabetes diagnosis, monitoring, and continuity of care, potentially affecting treatment outcomes in individuals with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes. This study aimed to evaluate treatment success and identify factors associated with achieving individualized glycemic targets among adults diagnosed with type 2 diabetes during the COVID-19 pandemic, with consideration of prior COVID-19 infection. Methods This single-center cross-sectional study included 211 adults diagnosed with type 2 diabetes after March 2020 and evaluated at a diabetes center in Türkiye between June and September 2023. Clinical, laboratory, treatment, and COVID-19 data were obtained from patient interviews and electronic health records. Treatment success was defined as achievement of individualized HbA1c targets according to the 2022 Turkish Endocrinology and Metabolism Society guideline. After excluding 20 participants who developed COVID-19 following diabetes diagnosis, factors associated with treatment success were evaluated in 191 participants using multivariable Firth penalized logistic regression, with additional models examining comorbidities and concomitant medication use as sensitivity analyses. Results Among 191 participants included in the treatment-success analysis, 139 (72.8%) achieved their individualized HbA1c target. In the primary Firth penalized logistic regression model, higher HbA1c at diagnosis was associated with lower odds of treatment success (aOR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66–0.97), whereas longer diabetes duration (aOR 1.06 per month, 95% CI 1.01–1.11) and pharmacological adherence (aOR 6.88, 95% CI 2.83–17.92) were associated with higher odds of success. Prior COVID-19 infection was also associated with higher odds of treatment success (aOR 2.88, 95% CI 1.15–8.04), although this finding should be interpreted cautiously. Conclusions Treatment success was primarily associated with baseline glycemic status and pharmacological adherence. The unexpected association between prior COVID-19 infection and higher odds of treatment success should be interpreted cautiously given its sensitivity to model specification. These findings emphasize the importance of treatment adherence and continuity of diabetes care.

title: Impact of COVID-19 on gastrointestinal disease in vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals: a population-based cohort study in England.
abstract: COVID-19 is associated with higher rates of gastrointestinal diseases, although the duration of this effect and the roles of vaccination and COVID-19 severity remain uncertain. To investigate the relationship between COVID-19 and gastrointestinal diseases by vaccination status in hospitalised and non-hospitalised patients. With NHS England approval, OpenSAFELY-TPP was used to access linked data from 24 million English adults. We defined three cohorts: 'prevaccination' (January 2020-June 2021), 'vaccinated' and 'unvaccinated' (June-December 2021). We estimated adjusted HRs (aHRs) comparing the incidence of 10 gastrointestinal diseases, including upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeding, after vs before or without a COVID-19 diagnosis overall and by COVID-19 severity. COVID-19 diagnosis was associated with elevated incidence of gastrointestinal diseases, particularly after hospitalised disease. In the prevaccination cohort (n=18 422 781), the aHRs for upper gastrointestinal bleeding after hospitalised COVID-19 were 20.1 (95% CI 18.4 to 22.1) in weeks 1-4 and 1.90 (1.63 to 2.22) in weeks 53-102. The corresponding aHRs after non-hospitalised COVID-19 were 1.92 (1.74 to 2.11) and 1.34 (1.23 to 1.45), respectively. Across time periods, aHRs for gastrointestinal diseases were lower in vaccinated (n=14 948 727) than in unvaccinated (n=3 479 043) individuals. These patterns were similar across gastrointestinal diseases. The incidence of gastrointestinal disease is elevated for up to 2 years among individuals hospitalised following a COVID-19 diagnosis, especially in the first few weeks after diagnosis. Increases in incidence are attenuated among vaccinated individuals. Monitoring for gastrointestinal diseases after severe COVID-19 and promotion of vaccination in vulnerable groups are key to reducing long-term burden.

title: Development of a robust T cell assay to retrospectively diagnose SARS-CoV-2 infection and T cell cytokine release assay as diagnostic and monitoring assay in Long COVID patients – COV-LT2-0004
abstract: Plain English Summary We aimed to understand the changes in the immune systems of patients with Long Covid to achieve two goals: (1) develop treatments for Long Covid and (2) provide objective ways to diagnose Long Covid. In our study, we discovered that the immune cells of Long Covid patients produce a protein called interferon gamma (IFN-γ). Typically, the immune system produces IFN-γ at the start of an infection to combat the virus, but stops once the virus is cleared. We observed that all COVID-19 patients produced IFN-γ during the infection, but this production ceased in most people once they recovered. However, in Long Covid patients, IFN-γ production continued. This indicates that the immune system in Long Covid patients behaves as if it’s in the early days of infection for months or even years. Since IFN-γ is associated with symptoms like fatigue, brain fog, and fever, we believe it may contribute to Long Covid symptoms. Future treatments could target IFN-γ in Long Covid patients. For the second goal, diagnosing Long Covid is challenging because some patients cannot prove they were infected with SARS-CoV-2 in the first place. This could be due to the lack of testing when they were initially sick or receiving false-negative test results. However, anyone infected with a virus retains immune memory of that virus. We developed a test that detects immune memory to SARS-CoV-2 in Long Covid patients, providing evidence of past infection and confirming their Long Covid diagnosis. Executive Summary Study aims: set up a clinic in May 2020, at Addenbrooke’s hospital, specifically for non-hospitalised Long Covid patients. Participants were enrolled into the Cambridge NIHR COVID Bioresource, blood samples for sera and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) were collected and BioBanked. The pilot data showed that PBMC produce interleukin-2 (IL-2) responses specific to nucleocapsid (N) and membrane (M) SARS-CoV-2 peptides are indicative of past SARS-CoV-2 infection. We were also surprised at the time to discover that PBMCs from patients with Long Covid were making interferon gamma (IFN-γ) spontaneously, without any stimulation.The study aimed to continue recruiting patients to the clinic every 3 months for up to 18 months. We wanted to a) confirm that the measurement of N and M specific T cell IL-2 production is a robust assay for the retrospective diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection and b) utilise spontaneous IFN-γ production as a monitoring biomarker for Long Covid patients. After achieving this, we aimed to c) adapt the approach to a simpler whole blood peptide stimulation assay with IFN-γ and IL-2 ELISA readouts that would be high throughput and easier to implement as clinical diagnostic assay. Background: More than half the UK population have had a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection, according to the Office for National Statistics. A significant minority of these infected people will go on to have continuing symptoms at least 3 months after infection, termed Long Covid. Rates of Long Covid depend on the thresholds chosen for diagnosis, age and infection severity, and are estimated to occur anywhere between 0.2-80% of infections. Currently people with Long Covid lack treatment options and struggle to get a diagnosis, due to a lack of supporting biomarkers. When we started this project in 2020 there were key clinical questions which needed addressing: 1. What are the causes of Long Covid symptoms and could understanding these causes lead to treatments? Are there potential biomarkers which could be used to diagnose Long Covid and differentiate it from conditions with similar symptom profiles? A diagnosis of Long Covid requires evidence of prior SARS-CoV-2 infection, however many people do not get tested when initially infected, and have antibody levels below detectability, leaving no evidence of infection. Can we use memory T cell responses to retrospectively diagnose COVID-19 and thereby provide evidence to support Long Covid diagnoses? PBMCs from the blood collected in citrate tubes was used for dual cytokine (IFN-γ and IL-2) T cell Fluorospot analysis of specific T cell responses to for Spike (S), Nucleocapsid (N) and Membrane (M) peptides. For additional controls we use a) CEF (CMV, EBV and Influenza) peptide mix for internal control; b) anti-CD3 and SEB (staphylococcal superantigen) mix – internal positive control and c) cells in media alone – internal negative control. The EDTA Trucount tubes were used to perform detailed cell phenotyping of the immune cell composition of patients with Long Covid and healthy controls. Markers included CD14, CD3, CD4, CD8, CD38, HLA-DR, CD69, NKG2D expression as well as markers of exhaustion. The RNA Paxgene tubes were utilised to perform single cell RNASeq on circulating immune cells for a detailed analysis of transcription profile in patients with Long Covid. The heparin treated whole blood was stimulated with peptides as with the fluorospot analyses above. IFN-γ and IL-2 production were measured by Enzyme Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA). Additionally, we used Legendplex analysis to measure with high throughput the cytokines produced by isolated PBMCs from patients with Long Covid and healthy controls. We also measured antibody levels over time in patients after SARS-CoV-2 infection using standard ELISA assays. We found that T cell responses to SARS-CoV-2 were a stronger and more reliable indicator of past SARS-CoV-2 infection than antibody levels. We were also able to adapt our initial T cell assay (a Fluorospot approach) into a quicker and cheaper ELISA assay. We also found that IFN-γ production is a key marker of Long Covid symptoms. IFN-γ production continues during the course of Long Covid but does return to normal levels in patients who recover from Long Covid.3. Our initial aim had been to recruit 500 Long Covid patients for our study and to follow up every 3 months for the 18 months of the study duration. This estimate was based on the 85 patients we initially recruited between May and December 2020 with an expectation of more patients arriving when lockdowns ended, which would lead to more infections, as well as an awareness campaign targeted towards general practitioners to refer patients to the Long Covid clinic for specialist treatment. However, we found that from August 2021 onwards there was a drop in referrals to the Long Covid clinic from across the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough area. We attribute this to vaccinations, which we believe reduced the number of COVID-19 infections, incidence of Long Covid and severity of Long Covid symptoms, causing a reduction in referrals. Key findings, including headline messages relevant to policy makers, conclusions and recommendations for further research: We hope that our T cell-based approach could be adopted by clinicians and used to retrospectively diagnose SARS-CoV-2 in the clinic to quickly confirm past infection to support Long Covid diagnosis. We also hope that future researchers might focus on IFN-γ as a therapeutic target or as a biomarker for Long Covid to support diagnosis. Finally, we hope that future research will consider how vaccination status affects Long Covid risk, and whether this is maintained over time. This is particularly important as Long Covid rates could rise in the future with the cessation of booster vaccines for most of the population. Dissemination plans: Most of the research findings have now been published (Krishna et al eBioMedicine 2022, Krishna et al CID 2023, Krishna et al Science Advances 2024). Two final manuscripts following up on the initial work have been produced and we are preparing them for submission to peer-reviewed journals. We have also had significant media interest in our work, and we have used these opportunities to highlight the continued suffering of patients with Long Covid. Expected influence/impact: We expect that our work will provide the foundations for changes in clinical practise, making it easier to diagnose patients with Long Covid and hopefully also highlight potential therapeutic options.

title: Sex-specific associations of ACE2 variants with COVID-19 hospitalization, viral load, and mortality: an Iranian hospital-based case-control study
abstract: Abstract Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 ( ACE2 ) is the cellular receptor for SARS-CoV-2, and its genetic polymorphisms may influence COVID-19 susceptibility. This hospital-based case-control study investigated the association between three ACE2 SNPs (rs2285666, rs4646127, rs971249) and normalized viral load, as well as risk of hospitalization for SARS-CoV-2 infection (comparing hospitalized COVID-19 patients versus hospitalized SARS-CoV-2-negative patients with other severe acute conditions), in 441 participants (226 cases, 215 hospital controls). Genotyping was performed by PCR-RFLP, and viral load was quantified by qRT-PCR and normalized to the RNase P gene. Associations were assessed using sex-stratified logistic regression with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing. In females, the rs971249 T allele showed a trend toward higher frequency in controls (48.9% vs. 39.5%; raw p = 0.007), but this association did not remain significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q = 0.12). In males, the T alleles of rs971249 and rs4646127 were associated with reduced infection risk and remained significant after correction for multiple testing (raw p = 0.003, q = 0.048 and raw p = 0.002, q = 0.036, respectively). No significant associations were observed for rs2285666. While no ACE2 polymorphism was significantly associated with normalized viral load after correction for multiple testing (all q > 0.05), rs971249 showed a trend toward higher viral load in heterozygous females that did not reach statistical significance (raw p = 0.052; q = 0.18). For mortality analysis, the reported associations for rs971249 and rs4646127 in females (adjusted OR = 2.54 and 2.73, respectively) are based on covariate-adjusted logistic regression (age, comorbidities, sampling time) but did not undergo Benjamini-Hochberg correction due to the exploratory nature of this subgroup analysis; these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and are clearly labeled as ‘nominally significant’ in the Results section (raw p < 0.05). However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the limited sample size and the exploratory nature of the subgroup analyses and because the rs971249 variant deviated from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in female controls ( p = 0.010). These findings suggest that the rs971249 and rs4646127 T alleles may confer sex-specific protection against hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 infection in this cohort of hospitalized patients. However, because controls were hospitalized patients with severe non-COVID-19 conditions, these associations reflect differences between two hospitalized groups rather than population-level susceptibility. Therefore, large-scale studies with population-based controls and diverse ethnic groups are warranted to validate these sex-specific associations and to clarify the role of ACE2 variants in population-level COVID-19 susceptibility.

title: Patient-month modeling for longitudinal blood culture contamination surveillance during a major healthcare-system disruption: a single-center interrupted time-series study.
abstract: Introduction Blood culture contamination (BCC) is an important diagnostic quality indicator, but crude temporal comparisons may be misleading when repeated sampling within patients is not considered. We evaluated longitudinal changes in BCC rates before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic using patient-month Poisson generalized estimating equations (GEE). Methods This single-center retrospective study included blood culture sets obtained at a tertiary hospital in Japan from April 2017 to June 2025. Eligible episodes had at least two sets drawn within 24 h. Interrupted time-series analysis estimated incidence rate ratios (IRRs) for level and slope changes at pandemic and post-reclassification transitions, with the number of sets as an offset and adjustment for seasonality and within-patient correlation. Results Among 85,955 blood culture sets, 84,213 sets from 41,732 episodes in 23,705 patients were analyzed. Crude BCC rates were 1.05%, 1.55%, and 1.49% in the prepandemic, pandemic, and post-reclassification periods. No significant overall level or slope changes were observed: prepandemic-to-pandemic level-change IRR, 1.23 (95% CI, 0.93-1.62); slope-change IRR, 1.00 (95% CI, 0.99-1.01); pandemic-to-post-reclassification level-change IRR, 0.88 (95% CI, 0.68-1.14); and slope-change IRR, 0.99 (95% CI, 0.98-1.01). Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested setting-specific post-reclassification changes in the intensive care unit. Sensitivity analyses were generally consistent, although the Omicron-era breakpoint analysis suggested sensitivity to breakpoint specification. Conclusion Patient-month Poisson GEE-based analysis showed that crude increases in BCC rates were not accompanied by statistically significant overall level or slope changes after accounting for repeated patient-level sampling and seasonality. Crude BCC trends should therefore be interpreted cautiously in longitudinal microbiology surveillance.

title: An Orthogonal Computational Framework Identifies a Conserved RNA Motif in the SARS-CoV-2 Spike Gene
abstract: Background: Structured RNA elements in viral genomes are underexplored therapeutic targets, yet coding regions have not been systematically screened for conserved, structurally defined motifs. Methods: We screened the SARS-CoV-2 spike coding sequence across eight major variants using a staged pipeline combining thermodynamic scanning, secondary-structure cross-validation between physics-based and deep-learning predictors, tertiary prediction across seven tools with decoy-controlled analogy searches, comparison with genome-wide chemical-probing data from three laboratories, and molecular dynamics simulation. Results: The screen identified three conserved, window-robust loci at functionally important spike regions: near the N343 glycosylation site (Region A), the E484 receptor-binding motif (Region B), and the S2′ cleavage site (Region C). Only Region A satisfied all thermodynamic and structural criteria, with a dinucleotide-shuffle z-score of −3.39 (p = 0.020), near-identical secondary structure between RNAfold and MXfold2 (F1 = 0.99), and a best-supported tertiary fold from convergence of Boltz-2 and AlphaFold3 (TM-score_RNA = 0.53). In-cell chemical-probing supported Region A (F1 = 0.83–0.85; AUROC = 0.663–0.892), while Regions B and C failed. Probing data refined the predicted fold to a two-helix architecture with a flexible middle segment, and molecular dynamics of the 101 nt window revealed two individually stable domains (3′ stem-loop RMSD = 2.58 ± 0.53 Å; 5′ helix RMSD = 4.65 ± 1.30 Å) joined by a mobile hinge. Conclusions: Region A is a conserved, structurally defined RNA element within the spike coding sequence, supported by several lines of evidence of differing independence. Its biological function and target-ligand compatibility remain unproven, and it warrants functional investigation as a previously underexplored RNA feature of a gene studied mainly at the protein level. The staged framework should be applicable to coding regions beyond SARS-CoV-2.
